title: Chapter 1: Introduction to React
summary: Understand what React is, why it exists, how the Virtual DOM makes it fast, and how to scaffold your first project with Vite.
content:
## What Is React? **React** is an open-source JavaScript library created by Meta in 2013. It is used to build fast, interactive User Interfaces (UIs), especially for Single Page Applications (SPAs). > Think of React like LEGO blocks. Each block is a "component" — like a button, a card, or a navbar. You snap these blocks together to build any UI you want. --- ## Why Use React? - Manually updating the DOM is slow and error-prone — React uses a **Virtual DOM** to batch and optimize updates - Code becomes hard to manage as apps grow — React enforces **component-based architecture** - Hard to reuse UI code — components are **reusable** by nature - State management is complex — React has built-in hooks for state --- ## How the Virtual DOM Works ```text // How React updates the UI efficiently Your Data Changes ↓ React creates a new Virtual DOM tree (lightweight JS object) ↓ React compares new tree vs old tree (Diffing Algorithm) ↓ React calculates the minimum real DOM changes needed ↓ React updates ONLY those specific parts of the real DOM ``` This process is called **Reconciliation**. It's much faster than replacing entire DOM sections manually. --- ## Setting Up Your First Project ```bash // Create and launch your first React project with Vite npm create vite@latest my-react-app -- --template react cd my-react-app npm install npm run dev ``` Your app runs at http://localhost:5173 --- ## Project Structure ```text // Vite React project file structure my-react-app/ ├── public/ ← Static assets ├── src/ │ ├── App.jsx ← Root component │ ├── main.jsx ← Entry point │ └── index.css ← Global styles ├── index.html ← HTML template └── package.json ← Dependencies ``` --- ## Your First React Code ```jsx // main.jsx — The Entry Point import React from 'react' import ReactDOM from 'react-dom/client' import App from './App.jsx' ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render( , ) ``` ```jsx // App.jsx — The Root Component function App() { return (

Hello, React! 🚀

My first React application.

) } export default App ``` --- ## Chapter Summary - React is a **UI library** for building component-based interfaces - The **Virtual DOM** makes React fast by minimizing real DOM updates - Use **Vite** to quickly scaffold a new React project - `main.jsx` mounts the app; `App.jsx` is the root component

tryItChallenge: Build a stopwatch using useRef to store the interval ID (instead of state) so it doesn't cause re-renders. Use useReducer for the stopwatch state machine with actions: START, PAUSE, RESET, TICK. Display elapsed time formatted as MM:SS.

When they click Search, fetch from https://api.github.com/users/{username} and display the user's avatar, name, bio, followers, and public repos count. Show a loading spinner during the fetch and an error message if the user is not found.

title: Chapter 13: Forms & Validation

Validate all fields on submit (no empty fields, valid email format, password min 8 chars, passwords must match, must accept terms). Show inline error messages next to each field. Show a success message when all validations pass.

title: Chapter 14: Custom Hooks

When the component mounts, it reads the saved value from localStorage. Whenever the state changes, it saves the new value. Test it with a theme preference that survives page refreshes.

Apply useMemo to the filter, React.memo to the list item component, and useCallback to the onChange handler. Use React DevTools Profiler to compare render counts before and after.

tryItChallenge: Convert a JavaScript React component — a UserCard that accepts name (string), age (number), role (string), and isActive (boolean) props — to TypeScript. Define a Props interface, type the component's return value as JSX.Element, and add a typed useState for a toggle state inside the component.

Test: (1) it renders with an initial count of 0, (2) clicking + increments the count, (3) clicking - decrements the count, (4) clicking - when count is 0 does not go below 0. title: Chapter 20: React Project Structure & Best Practices
summary: Learn how professional teams organize large React codebases, write clean readable code, and follow conventions that make apps easy to maintain and scale.
content:
## Why Project Structure Matters As apps grow, bad structure creates: - Files that are impossible to find - Circular dependencies - Components that are impossible to test - Fear of refactoring (you don't know what will break) Good structure gives you **confidence to change things quickly**. --- ## Feature-Based Folder Structure (Recommended) ```text src/ ├── features/ ← Each feature is self-contained │ ├── auth/ │ │ ├── components/ ← Auth-specific components │ │ │ ├── LoginForm.jsx │ │ │ └── SignupForm.jsx │ │ ├── hooks/ ← Auth-specific hooks │ │ │ └── useAuth.js │ │ ├── store/ ← Auth state (Zustand/Context) │ │ │ └── authStore.js │ │ ├── api/ ← Auth API calls │ │ │ └── authApi.js │ │ └── index.js ← Public API of this feature │ │ │ ├── products/ │ │ ├── components/ │ │ ├── hooks/ │ │ └── index.js │ │ │ └── cart/ │ ├── components/ │ ├── store/ │ └── index.js │ ├── shared/ ← Reusable across features │ ├── components/ │ │ ├── Button.jsx │ │ ├── Input.jsx │ │ ├── Modal.jsx │ │ └── index.js │ ├── hooks/ │ │ ├── useFetch.js │ │ ├── useDebounce.js │ │ └── index.js │ └── utils/ │ ├── formatDate.js │ └── validators.js │ ├── pages/ (or app/ in Next.js) ├── lib/ ← Third-party config (axios instance, etc.) └── types/ ← TypeScript type definitions ``` --- ## Barrel Exports (index.js) ```js // shared/components/index.js — export everything from one place export { default as Button } from './Button' export { default as Input } from './Input' export { default as Modal } from './Modal' export { default as Card } from './Card' ``` ```jsx // Now import from the folder, not the file // ❌ Messy imports import Button from '../../shared/components/Button' import Input from '../../shared/components/Input' import Modal from '../../shared/components/Modal' // ✅ Clean barrel imports import { Button, Input, Modal } from '@/shared/components' ``` --- ## Component File Structure ```jsx // features/products/components/ProductCard.jsx // Standard structure for every component file: // 1. Imports (external libs first, then internal) import { useState, memo } from 'react' import { ShoppingCart, Star } from 'lucide-react' import { Button } from '@/shared/components' import { useCartStore } from '@/features/cart' import styles from './ProductCard.module.css' // 2. TypeScript types / PropTypes interface ProductCardProps { id: number name: string price: number rating: number image: string } // 3. Component (named export preferred) export function ProductCard({ id, name, price, rating, image }: ProductCardProps) { const [added, setAdded] = useState(false) const addToCart = useCartStore(state => state.addItem) function handleAddToCart() { addToCart({ id, name, price }) setAdded(true) setTimeout(() => setAdded(false), 2000) } return (

{name}

{rating}/5

${price}

) } // 4. Default export (optional, some teams use only named exports) export default memo(ProductCard) ``` --- ## Naming Conventions ```text Files & Folders: Components → PascalCase.jsx (UserCard.jsx, Button.jsx) Hooks → camelCase.js (useFetch.js, useAuth.js) Utilities → camelCase.js (formatDate.js, validators.js) Stores → camelCase.js (authStore.js, cartStore.js) CSS Modules → PascalCase.module.css Variables & Functions: Components → PascalCase (function UserCard) Hooks → use + PascalCase (function useLocalStorage) Event handlers → handle + Event (handleSubmit, handleClick) Boolean state → is/has/can prefix (isLoading, hasError, canSubmit) Constants → SCREAMING_SNAKE (MAX_RETRIES, API_BASE_URL) ``` --- ## Code Quality Rules ```jsx // 1. One component per file // ❌ Multiple components crammed into one file // ✅ Each component has its own file // 2. Keep components small — if it's > 150 lines, split it // ❌ 400-line mega-component // ✅ Parent + 3-4 focused child components // 3. Don't duplicate logic — extract to a custom hook // ❌ Same fetch logic in 4 components // ✅ useFetch hook used in all 4 // 4. Never hardcode values in JSX — use constants or config // ❌ // ✅ const MAX_IMAGE_WIDTH = '320px' // 5. Prefer named exports for components (easier to find with IDE) // ❌ export default function () { ... } // ✅ export function ProductCard() { ... } // 6. Avoid prop drilling beyond 2 levels — use Context or Zustand // 7. Co-locate state as close to where it's used as possible // 8. Write self-documenting code — names should explain intent ``` --- ## ESLint + Prettier Setup ```bash // Install ESLint and Prettier for automatic code quality npm install -D eslint prettier eslint-config-prettier eslint-plugin-react eslint-plugin-react-hooks ``` ```json // .eslintrc.json { "extends": [ "eslint:recommended", "plugin:react/recommended", "plugin:react-hooks/recommended", "prettier" ], "rules": { "react/prop-types": "off", "react/react-in-jsx-scope": "off", "no-unused-vars": "warn", "react-hooks/exhaustive-deps": "warn" } } ``` ```json // .prettierrc { "semi": false, "singleQuote": true, "tabWidth": 2, "trailingComma": "es5", "printWidth": 100 } ``` --- ## Chapter Summary - Use **feature-based folders** — each feature owns its components, hooks, and state - Use **barrel exports** (`index.js`) to simplify imports across the codebase - Follow consistent naming: PascalCase for components, camelCase for hooks/utils - Keep components small and focused — split when > 150 lines - Set up **ESLint + Prettier** early to enforce consistency automatically - Co-locate related code — don't scatter a feature's files across unrelated folders

title: Chapter 22: Deployment & Going to Production
summary: Deploy your React app to the internet using Vercel and Netlify, configure environment variables, set up CI/CD pipelines, and apply production best practices.
content: ## Production Checklist Before deploying any React app, make sure: ```text ✅ No console.log() left in production code ✅ All API URLs use environment variables (not hardcoded) ✅ Error boundaries added to catch runtime crashes gracefully ✅ 404 and loading states handled for all data fetches ✅ Images optimized (WebP format, correct dimensions) ✅ and meta description set for each page ✅ npm run build completes without errors ✅ All environment variables documented in .env.example ``` --- ## Environment Variables ```bash # .env.local — for local development (never commit this!) VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:5000/api/v1 VITE_APP_NAME=MyApp # .env.production — for production builds VITE_API_URL=https://api.myapp.com/v1 VITE_APP_NAME=MyApp # .env.example — commit this! Documents all required vars VITE_API_URL=https://your-api-url.com/api/v1 VITE_APP_NAME=YourAppName ``` ```jsx // In your React code — always use import.meta.env for Vite const API_URL = import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL const APP_NAME = import.meta.env.VITE_APP_NAME // For Create React App, it's process.env.REACT_APP_API_URL // ⚠️ IMPORTANT: // - Vite: vars MUST start with VITE_ // - CRA: vars MUST start with REACT_APP_ // - Any other prefix and the variable will be undefined in the browser ``` --- ## Building for Production ```bash // Build your app for production npm run build // What this does: // 1. Compiles all JSX/TSX to optimized JavaScript // 2. Bundles and minifies all files // 3. Splits code into smaller chunks (code splitting) // 4. Outputs to the /dist folder // Preview the production build locally npm run preview // Opens http://localhost:4173 — this is exactly what users will see ``` --- ## Deploy to Vercel (Recommended) ```bash // Option A: Deploy via CLI npm install -g vercel vercel login vercel // Follow the prompts — done in ~60 seconds! ``` ```text Option B: Deploy via GitHub (recommended for teams) 1. Push your code to GitHub 2. Go to vercel.com → New Project → Import Git Repository 3. Select your repo 4. Vercel auto-detects Vite/React settings 5. Add environment variables in the dashboard 6. Click Deploy After that: every push to main auto-deploys. Every pull request gets its own preview URL. ``` --- ## Deploy to Netlify ```bash // Option A: CLI npm install -g netlify-cli netlify login npm run build netlify deploy --prod --dir=dist ``` ```text Option B: GitHub integration 1. Push to GitHub 2. netlify.com → New site from Git → Choose repo 3. Build command: npm run build 4. Publish directory: dist 5. Add env vars in Site Settings → Environment variables 6. Deploy! ``` --- ## Fix Client-Side Routing on Netlify ```text // Problem: Navigating to /about directly returns 404 on Netlify // (The server doesn't know about React Router routes) // Fix: Create public/_redirects file /* /index.html 200 // Or netlify.toml in project root: ``` ```toml # netlify.toml [[redirects]] from = "/*" to = "/index.html" status = 200 ``` ```text // Vercel handles this automatically — no config needed ``` --- ## Error Boundaries — Catch Crashes Gracefully ```jsx // components/ErrorBoundary.jsx // Catches JavaScript errors anywhere in the child component tree import { Component } from 'react' class ErrorBoundary extends Component { constructor(props) { super(props) this.state = { hasError: false, error: null } } static getDerivedStateFromError(error) { return { hasError: true, error } } componentDidCatch(error, info) { // Log to your error tracking service (Sentry, etc.) console.error('Caught error:', error, info.componentStack) } render() { if (this.state.hasError) { return ( <div style={{ textAlign: 'center', padding: '48px' }}> <h2>Something went wrong</h2> <p>{this.state.error?.message}</p> <button onClick={() => this.setState({ hasError: false, error: null })}> Try Again </button> </div> ) } return this.props.children } } export default ErrorBoundary ``` ```jsx // Wrap your app with ErrorBoundary import ErrorBoundary from './components/ErrorBoundary' function App() { return ( <ErrorBoundary> <Router> <AppContent /> </Router> </ErrorBoundary> ) } ``` --- ## Performance: Analyzing Your Bundle ```bash // See what's making your bundle large npm install -D rollup-plugin-visualizer // Add to vite.config.js: import { visualizer } from 'rollup-plugin-visualizer' export default defineConfig({ plugins: [ react(), visualizer({ open: true }) // Opens a visual bundle map after build ] }) npm run build // A browser window opens showing you which packages are largest // Look for: unexpectedly large dependencies you could replace or lazy-load ``` --- ## Setting Up Sentry for Error Tracking ```bash npm install @sentry/react ``` ```jsx // main.jsx — initialize Sentry before rendering import * as Sentry from "@sentry/react" Sentry.init({ dsn: import.meta.env.VITE_SENTRY_DSN, environment: import.meta.env.MODE, // "development" or "production" tracesSampleRate: 0.1, // Send 10% of transactions to Sentry }) ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render( <React.StrictMode> <App /> </React.StrictMode> ) // Now any unhandled error in production is captured in your Sentry dashboard ``` --- ## CI/CD with GitHub Actions ```yaml # .github/workflows/deploy.yml # Automatically test and deploy on every push to main name: CI/CD Pipeline on: push: branches: [main] pull_request: branches: [main] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: '20' - run: npm ci - run: npm test -- --run # Run tests once (not watch mode) - run: npm run build # Verify build succeeds # Vercel and Netlify auto-deploy on push via their GitHub integration # No extra deploy step needed if you've connected your repo to them ``` --- ## Chapter Summary - Run `npm run build` and test with `npm run preview` before deploying - Store secrets in environment variables — never hardcode API keys - Vite vars must start with `VITE_` to be accessible in the browser - **Vercel** is the easiest deployment platform for React/Next.js apps - **Netlify** requires a `_redirects` file for client-side routing to work - Wrap your app in an **ErrorBoundary** to catch and handle runtime crashes - Set up **Sentry** for production error monitoring - Use GitHub Actions for automated test + build checks on every PR --- ## Course Complete! Congratulations on completing the full React.js course! Here is everything you have learned: **Fundamentals:** JSX, Components, Props, State, Events, Lists, Conditional Rendering **Hooks:** useState, useEffect, useRef, useReducer, useMemo, useCallback, Custom Hooks **Routing:** React Router v6 — Routes, Params, Nested Routes, Navigation **State Management:** Context API, Zustand with persistence middleware **Data:** Fetching with fetch/axios, loading and error states, cancellation **Forms:** Controlled inputs, all input types, validation patterns **TypeScript:** Typed props, events, state, custom hooks, and context **Testing:** React Testing Library, Vitest, mocking API calls **Performance:** React.memo, useMemo, useCallback, lazy loading, virtualization **Architecture:** Feature-based structure, barrel exports, naming conventions, ESLint **Deployment:** Environment variables, Vercel, Netlify, Error Boundaries, CI/CD **Your next steps:** - Build projects — nothing teaches like shipping real apps - Learn Next.js deeply for full-stack React development - Explore React Native for mobile apps using your existing React knowledge - Contribute to open source — reading and improving real code is invaluable

title: What is Next.js? Why Next.js?
summary: Understand why Next.js exists, what problems it solves over plain React, and the key features that make it the gold standard for production React apps.
content:
## What is Next.js? Next.js is a **full-stack React framework** built by Vercel that adds powerful server-side capabilities, robust routing, and production-level optimizations to React. While React itself is merely a UI library that excels at managing state and rendering components in the browser, Next.js takes React and wraps it into a complete, opinionated architecture. When we say "framework" instead of "library", we mean that Next.js gives you a specific set of rules and folder structures to follow. In return, it handles all the complex plumbing—like routing, bundling, compiling, and server-side rendering—automatically. --- ## Why NOT Plain React? The Problems Next.js Solves If you have built apps with Create React App (CRA) or Vite + React, you were building **Client-Side Rendered (CSR)** applications. In a CSR app, the server sends a nearly empty HTML file (often just `
`) along with a massive JavaScript bundle. This approach creates several significant problems for production applications: ### 1. Poor Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Search engine crawlers (like Googlebot) traditionally struggle to index client-side rendered apps. When they request a plain React page, they see an empty `div`. While Google's crawler has gotten better at executing JavaScript, it's still slower, less reliable, and many social media link preview bots (like Twitter/X or iMessage) will simply show a blank preview. Next.js solves this by pre-rendering HTML on the server. ### 2. Slow Initial Page Load In plain React, the user sees a blank white screen until the entire React bundle is downloaded, parsed, and executed. This harms user experience, especially on slow mobile networks. ### 3. Routing Boilerplate In a standard React app, you must install and configure third-party libraries (like `react-router-dom`) and manually wire up your navigation logic. Next.js provides a robust **File-System Based Router** out of the box. ### 4. Need for a Separate Backend If your React app needs to talk to a database, you usually have to spin up a completely separate Express or NestJS server. Next.js allows you to write backend API endpoints and server-side logic directly in the same codebase. --- ## The Ultimate Comparison Here is a quick breakdown of how Next.js outshines a traditional Client-Side React setup: | Feature/Problem | Plain React (Vite / CRA) | Next.js (App Router) | |---|---|---| | **SEO & Crawlers** | Poor (Client-side rendering only) | Excellent (HTML is pre-rendered on the server) | | **Initial Load Speed** | Slower (Waits for JS bundle) | Faster (User sees HTML immediately) | | **Routing** | Manual setup (react-router) | Automatic File-System Routing | | **Data Fetching** | Fetch on mount (waterfall issues) | Native Server Components & Server Actions | | **Backend / APIs** | Requires separate Node.js server | Built-in Route Handlers and Server Actions | | **Image Optimization** | Manual handling required | Automatic WebP/AVIF via `` | | **Code Splitting** | Requires manual `React.lazy()` | Automatic per-page code splitting | --- ## The Two Eras of Next.js: Pages vs App Router As you learn Next.js, you will encounter two different routing paradigms. It is critical to understand the difference: ### 1. The Pages Router (Legacy, Next.js 12 and below) Historically, Next.js used the `pages/` directory. You would fetch data using specialized functions like `getServerSideProps` (for SSR) and `getStaticProps` (for SSG). While still fully supported, this is now considered the older way of building apps. ### 2. The App Router (Modern, Next.js 13+) Introduced recently, the `app/` directory represents a massive paradigm shift. It is built entirely around **React Server Components (RSC)**. By default, every component you write runs *only on the server*. This eliminates the need for `getServerSideProps` and drastically reduces the amount of JavaScript sent to the browser. > **Important Note:** This course focuses entirely on the modern **App Router**, as it is the future of React development. --- ## The Core Capabilities of Next.js 1. **Server-Side Rendering (SSR):** Generates HTML on the server for *every single request*. Perfect for highly dynamic data that changes constantly (like a user dashboard). 2. **Static Site Generation (SSG):** Generates HTML once at *build time*. Perfect for marketing pages and blogs, resulting in lightning-fast, CDN-cacheable pages. 3. **Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR):** A hybrid approach where static pages are rebuilt in the background on a timer, without needing a full site redeploy. 4. **React Server Components:** Components that fetch data and render securely on the server, never exposing their code or sensitive API keys to the browser. --- ## When Should You Use Next.js? Next.js is incredibly versatile, but it shines the brightest in these scenarios: - **E-Commerce Platforms:** Where SEO, initial load times, and dynamic pricing are critical. - **Content Heavy Sites:** Blogs, news outlets, and documentation sites. - **SaaS Applications:** Dashboards that require secure data fetching and complex authentication flows. - **Full-Stack MVPs:** When you want to move fast without managing separate frontend and backend repositories. ## Summary Next.js takes the UI power of React and adds the missing pieces required for serious, production-grade applications. It shifts the heavy lifting from the user's browser back to the server, resulting in faster, more secure, and highly discoverable applications.

title: Setting Up Your First Next.js Project
summary: Scaffold a new Next.js 14+ project using create-next-app, understand the project structure, and run your first dev server.
content:
## Creating a New Next.js Project The fastest and most reliable way to start a Next.js project is with the official CLI tool called `create-next-app`. ```bash npx create-next-app@latest my-app ``` When you run this command, Next.js will prompt you with several architectural choices: ``` Would you like to use TypeScript? Yes Would you like to use ESLint? Yes Would you like to use Tailwind CSS? Yes Would you like to use src/ directory? Yes Would you like to use App Router? Yes Would you like to customize the default import alias? No ``` > **Interview Highlight** > **Q: What is the `src/` directory used for in Next.js?** > A: The `src/` directory is an optional but highly recommended convention to separate your application's source code from configuration files (like `.env`, `next.config.mjs`, `package.json`) that live in the project root. It prevents accidental exposure of config files and keeps the root clean. --- ## Project Structure Explained After creation, your folder structure looks like this: ``` my-app/ ├── public/ ← Static assets (images, fonts, icons) ├── src/ │ └── app/ │ ├── layout.jsx ← Root layout (wraps all pages) │ ├── page.jsx ← Home page (route: /) │ └── globals.css ← Global CSS ├── next.config.mjs ← Next.js configuration ├── package.json └── jsconfig.json ← Path aliases (@/ -> src/) ``` > **Definition: The `public/` Directory** > Any file placed in the `public` folder is served directly at the root URL path. For example, `public/logo.png` is accessible via `http://localhost:3000/logo.png`. This is where you store static files like favicons, robots.txt, and raw images. --- ## Key Files Explained ### src/app/layout.jsx — The Root Layout The root layout is a **required** file in the App Router. It defines the global HTML structure. ```jsx export const metadata = { title: 'My App', description: 'My Next.js app', } export default function RootLayout({ children }) { return (
Global Navigation
{children} ) } ``` > **Interview Highlight** > **Q: Can a Next.js App Router application exist without a root `layout.jsx`?** > A: No. The App Router requires at least one root layout to define the `` and `` tags. If you delete it, Next.js will automatically generate a basic one for you on the next development server run. ### src/app/page.jsx — Home Page This file corresponds to your root URL (`/`). ```jsx export default function HomePage() { return

Hello, Next.js!

} ``` --- ## Running the Dev Server To start your application locally with Hot Module Replacement (HMR): ```bash cd my-app npm run dev ``` Visit **http://localhost:3000** — your app is live. When you save a file, the browser updates instantly without a full page refresh. --- ## Available Scripts (package.json) | Command | Purpose | When to use | |---|---|---| | `next dev` | Starts the development server with Hot Module Replacement (HMR) | When writing code locally | | `next build` | Compiles your app, optimizes assets, and creates an optimized production bundle | Before deploying to production | | `next start` | Starts a production Node.js server using the built bundle | To test the production build locally or run in Docker | | `next lint` | Runs ESLint to catch syntax and architectural errors | Before committing code | > **Definition: Next.js Compiler** > Next.js uses **SWC** (Speedy Web Compiler), a Rust-based compiler that replaces Babel and Terser. It is exponentially faster at compiling JavaScript/TypeScript and minifying code during `next build`. --- ## Path Aliases By default, Next.js configures the `@/` path alias in `jsconfig.json` or `tsconfig.json`. This maps to the root of your code (usually `src/`). **Why is this useful?** It prevents ugly relative import paths in deeply nested files. ```jsx // ❌ Bad (Brittle and hard to read) import Button from '../../../components/Button' // ✅ Good (Absolute alias) import Button from '@/components/Button' ``` ## Summary Setting up Next.js is zero-configuration. The framework establishes strong conventions out of the box—like the `public` folder for static assets and `@/` aliases—allowing developers to focus on writing application code rather than configuring Webpack or Babel.

title: File-Based Routing in the App Router
summary: Master how Next.js creates routes from your file system — pages, nested routes, dynamic routes, route groups, and more.
content:
## How File-Based Routing Works In the Next.js App Router, **the folder structure IS the routing structure**. Instead of declaring routes in a centralized `App.jsx` file (like in React Router), you define routes by creating folders inside the `src/app/` directory. > **Definition: File-Based Routing** > A routing mechanism where the framework automatically maps the file system hierarchy (folders and specific filenames) to URL paths. Every folder under `app/` that contains a `page.jsx` file becomes a publicly accessible URL route. --- ## Basic Routes & Nested Routes ``` src/app/ ├── page.jsx → / ├── about/ │ └── page.jsx → /about └── dashboard/ ├── page.jsx → /dashboard └── settings/ └── page.jsx → /dashboard/settings ``` If a folder does not contain a `page.jsx` file, it is **not routable**. This allows you to safely store components, styles, or utility functions alongside your routes without them accidentally becoming public URLs. --- ## Dynamic Routes — [param] When you don't know the exact segment name ahead of time (e.g., blog post slugs or user IDs), use square brackets to create dynamic routes. ``` src/app/ └── blog/ ├── page.jsx → /blog └── [slug]/ └── page.jsx → /blog/hello-world, /blog/any-post ``` ### Accessing the Dynamic Param Dynamic segments are passed as the `params` prop to your `page.jsx` component. ```jsx // src/app/blog/[slug]/page.jsx export default function BlogPost({ params }) { // If URL is /blog/nextjs-routing, params.slug is 'nextjs-routing' return

Post: {params.slug}

} ``` > **Interview Highlight** > **Q: What is the difference between Catch-All `[...slug]` and Optional Catch-All `[[...slug]]` routes?** > A: A Catch-All route (`app/docs/[...slug]/page.jsx`) will match `/docs/a`, `/docs/a/b`, etc., but **will 404 on `/docs`**. An Optional Catch-All route (`[[...slug]]`) will match all those nested paths **AND** the root `/docs` path. --- ## Route Groups — (groupName) You can group routes logically without affecting the URL path by wrapping a folder name in parentheses. ``` src/app/ ├── (marketing)/ │ ├── about/page.jsx → /about (URL is NOT /marketing/about) │ └── contact/page.jsx → /contact └── (app)/ ├── layout.jsx ← Layout applied only to /dashboard └── dashboard/ └── page.jsx → /dashboard ``` > **Definition: Route Groups** > A feature used to organize route segments into logical groups without adding them to the URL path. They are incredibly useful for applying different layouts to different sections of the app (e.g., a marketing layout vs. an authenticated dashboard layout) while keeping the URLs clean. --- ## Special Files in the App Router Next.js provides a set of special files to create UI for specific routing behaviors: | File | Purpose | |---|---| | `page.jsx` | Creates the unique UI for a route and makes the path publicly accessible. | | `layout.jsx` | Wraps the route and its children in shared UI. **Preserves state** on navigation. | | `template.jsx` | Similar to layout, but creates a **new instance** on navigation (good for enter animations). | | `loading.jsx` | Defines an automatic React Suspense fallback UI (e.g., a skeleton loader). | | `error.jsx` | Defines an Error Boundary UI. Must be a Client Component (`'use client'`). | | `not-found.jsx` | UI to show when a route is not found or when `notFound()` is thrown. | | `route.js` | Creates a backend API endpoint (HTTP handler). | --- ## Navigation: The `` Component Always use the Next.js `` component for navigation rather than standard HTML `` tags. ```jsx import Link from 'next/link' export default function Nav() { return (
Home About
) } ``` > **Interview Highlight** > **Q: Why should you use `` instead of `` in Next.js?** > A: `` enables client-side navigation between routes without a full page reload, maintaining application state. Furthermore, it automatically **prefetches** the linked page's code in the background when the link enters the viewport, making transitions near-instantaneous. --- ## Programmatic Navigation When you need to navigate after an action (like submitting a form), use the `useRouter` hook. ```jsx 'use client' import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation' export default function LoginButton() { const router = useRouter() return ( ) } ```

title: Layouts and Nested Layouts
summary: Learn how layout.jsx files create persistent UI shells that wrap your pages — headers, sidebars, footers that don't re-render on navigation.
content:
## What is a Layout? A `layout.jsx` file creates a UI shell that wraps its sibling `page.jsx` and all nested child routes. Unlike pages, **layouts do not re-render on navigation**. This means any state inside a layout (like a search input or an open sidebar) is preserved when users click between pages. > **Definition: Layout Component** > A React component that shares UI across multiple routes. On navigation, layouts preserve state, remain interactive, and do not re-render, enabling true Single Page Application (SPA) feel within a multi-page framework. --- ## The Root Layout (Required) Every Next.js App Router application must have a top-level root layout at `src/app/layout.jsx`. ```jsx // src/app/layout.jsx import './globals.css' export const metadata = { title: 'My App', description: 'My awesome Next.js app', } export default function RootLayout({ children }) { return (
My Global Header
{children}
My Global Footer
) } ``` The `{children}` prop is a placeholder where the specific page content (or nested layout content) gets injected. --- ## Nested Layouts Layouts can be deeply nested. When you put a `layout.jsx` inside a folder, it wraps all pages inside that folder and deeper, stacking inside the layouts above it. ``` src/app/ ├── layout.jsx ← Root layout (Outer shell: html, body, Header) ├── page.jsx ← Home: wrapped by Root layout └── dashboard/ ├── layout.jsx ← Dashboard layout (Inner shell: Sidebar) ├── page.jsx ← /dashboard: Sidebar + Root layout └── settings/ └── page.jsx ← /dashboard/settings: Sidebar + Root layout ``` > **Interview Highlight** > **Q: What happens to the DOM when you navigate from `/dashboard` to `/dashboard/settings`?** > A: The Root Layout and the Dashboard Layout do not re-render. Only the specific page component (`settings/page.jsx`) is fetched and swapped into the DOM. This prevents unnecessary network requests and preserves layout state (like scroll position). ### Example of a Nested Dashboard Layout ```jsx // src/app/dashboard/layout.jsx export default function DashboardLayout({ children }) { return (
Overview Settings
{children}
) } ``` --- ## Layouts vs Templates Next.js also provides a `template.jsx` file. It looks identical to a layout, but it behaves differently. | Feature | `layout.jsx` | `template.jsx` | |---|---|---| | **Re-renders on navigation?** | No | Yes (A new instance is mounted) | | **Preserves state?** | Yes | No (State is reset) | | **Primary Use Case** | Sidebars, Navigation, Footers | Enter/Exit CSS animations, resetting forms, tracking page views | > **Definition: Template File (`template.jsx`)** > A file that wraps a route segment similar to a layout, but creates a new DOM instance on navigation. Use it when you specifically *want* to trigger a re-render or reset state across route changes. --- ## Metadata in Layouts Layouts are an excellent place to define metadata templates. This avoids repeating the same site name on every page. ```jsx // src/app/dashboard/layout.jsx export const metadata = { title: { template: '%s | Dashboard', default: 'Dashboard Overview', } } ``` When a child page defines its own title: ```jsx // src/app/dashboard/settings/page.jsx export const metadata = { title: 'Settings', // The final title becomes: "Settings | Dashboard" } ``` --- ## Summary Layouts allow you to build complex, nested application shells. By preventing re-renders on navigation, layouts dramatically improve performance and user experience by preserving scroll position and UI state.

title: Next.js Image Optimization
summary: Use the powerful next/image component for automatic image optimization, lazy loading, responsive images, and preventing layout shift.
content:
## The Core Problem with Regular HTML `` Tags Images account for over 50% of the bytes downloaded on a typical website. Using a standard HTML `` tag causes massive performance issues: - **No Lazy Loading:** Browsers load off-screen images immediately, wasting bandwidth. - **Over-fetching:** Serving a massive 4K desktop image to a tiny mobile screen. - **Layout Shift:** Before an image loads, it takes up 0px. When it suddenly loads, it pushes all text down, violating Core Web Vitals (Cumulative Layout Shift). - **Outdated Formats:** Serving bulky PNG/JPEG instead of next-generation formats like WebP or AVIF. > **Definition: Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)** > A Google Core Web Vitals metric that measures how much elements move around the screen while the page is loading. A high CLS ruins user experience and hurts SEO. Next.js eliminates this automatically. --- ## The Next.js `` Solution The `next/image` component solves all these problems automatically out of the box. ```jsx import Image from 'next/image' import localPic from '@/public/hero-banner.jpg' // Importing local file export default function HeroSection() { return ( // Width and height are detected automatically from the local file! ) } ``` What Next.js does for you behind the scenes: - Automatically converts the image to **WebP** or **AVIF** (drastically reducing file size). - Injects a blurred placeholder (if configured) while the image loads. - Strictly enforces `width` and `height` constraints to ensure exactly **zero layout shift**. - Automatically delays loading (lazy loading) until the image is near the viewport viewport. --- ## Handling Remote Images If your images come from an external URL (like an S3 bucket or Unsplash), Next.js cannot auto-detect the dimensions, nor does it trust the source by default to prevent malicious bandwidth exhaustion. **Step 1: Configure allowed domains in `next.config.mjs`** ```js // next.config.mjs const nextConfig = { images: { remotePatterns: [ { protocol: 'https', hostname: 'images.unsplash.com', }, { protocol: 'https', hostname: '**.s3.amazonaws.com', // Wildcards supported }, ], }, } export default nextConfig ``` **Step 2: Explicitly provide `width` and `height`** ```jsx import Image from 'next/image' export default function Avatar({ user }) { return ( ) } ``` > **Interview Highlight** > **Q: Why does the Next.js Image component require `width` and `height` for remote images?** > A: To prevent Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS). By providing exact pixel dimensions, Next.js can render a placeholder box of the exact correct size on the server before the image even begins downloading. --- ## Fill Mode: When you don't know the exact size Sometimes you want an image to completely fill a fluid container (like a full-width background hero section). Instead of providing `width` and `height`, you use the `fill` prop. ```jsx
``` **CRITICAL RULE:** When using `fill`, the immediate parent element MUST have `position: relative`, `absolute`, or `fixed` applied via CSS. --- ## Priority Loading (LCP Optimization) Search engines judge your site heavily on **Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)** — the time it takes to render the largest visible element above the fold. By default, Next.js lazy-loads every image. If the user's viewport opens on a giant hero image, lazy loading it actually *hurts* performance. ```jsx /> ``` Always add the `priority` prop to any image that is immediately visible to the user without scrolling. --- ## Summary of Critical Props | Prop | Required? | Purpose | |---|---|---| | `src` | Yes | Image source (local import or URL string). | | `alt` | Yes | Accessibility description for screen readers and SEO. | | `width`/`height` | Yes (unless `fill`) | Intrinsic dimensions to prevent layout shift. | | `fill` | No | Tells the image to absolutely position itself to its parent container. | | `priority` | No | Preloads the image for immediate rendering. Crucial for LCP elements. | | `sizes` | No | Defines responsive breakpoints so the browser requests the right size file. |

title: Deploying Next.js to Production
summary: Deploy your Next.js app to Vercel, understand build output, Docker deployment, production optimizations, and the production readiness checklist.
content: ## Hosting Platforms Next.js is a full-stack framework requiring a Node.js server to run Server Components, SSR, and API Routes. | Platform | Difficulty | Pros | Cons | |---|---|---|---| | **Vercel** | ⭐ Extremely Easy | Zero-config, Edge network, Built by Next.js creators. | Can get expensive at massive scale. | | **Railway / Render** | ⭐⭐ Easy | Cheaper scaling, great for full-stack with attached databases. | No Edge network by default. | | **AWS / GCP / Docker** | ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Hard | Maximum control, cheapest at scale. | You manage CI/CD, SSL, and load balancing manually. | --- ## Deploying to Vercel (The Happy Path) Vercel provides the smoothest deployment experience. It automatically detects your Next.js project and sets up the CI/CD pipeline. **Steps to Deploy:** 1. Push your code to a GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket repository. 2. Log in to [Vercel.com](https://vercel.com). 3. Click **Add New Project** and import your repository. 4. Add your **Environment Variables** (e.g., `DATABASE_URL`, `AUTH_SECRET`) in the Vercel dashboard. 5. Click **Deploy**. Every time you push to the `main` branch, Vercel will automatically build and deploy your application. Pushes to other branches create instant "Preview Deployments" you can share with your team. --- ## Building Locally for Production Before pushing to production, you should ALWAYS build the project locally to catch compilation errors. ```bash npm run build ``` When the build finishes, Next.js outputs an incredibly important table. **You must learn how to read it.** ```text Route (app) Size First Load JS ┌ ○ / 5.2 kB 87.3 kB ├ ℇ /dashboard 2.1 kB 84.3 kB ├ ● /blog/[slug] 3.8 kB 86.0 kB └ ℇ /api/users 0 B 0 B ○ (Static) prerendered as static HTML (SSG) ● (SSG) prerendered as static HTML (uses generateStaticParams) ℇ (Dynamic) server-rendered on demand (SSR) ``` > **Interview Highlight** > **Q: What does the `○ (Static)` vs `ℇ (Dynamic)` symbol mean in the Next.js build output?** > A: `○ (Static)` means the page was fully rendered at build time into an HTML file (SSG) and can be served instantly from a CDN. `ℇ (Dynamic)` means the page uses dynamic functions (like reading cookies or URL parameters) and must be Server-Side Rendered (SSR) on every single request. --- ## Deploying via Docker (Self-Hosting) If you need to deploy Next.js to your own servers (e.g. AWS EC2, DigitalOcean), you should use Docker and enable **Standalone Output**. Normally, Next.js relies on your massive `node_modules` folder to run. Standalone mode traces your code and copies *only the exact files and dependencies needed* into a minimal folder, drastically reducing Docker image sizes. **Step 1:** Enable standalone mode in `next.config.mjs` ```js // next.config.mjs export default { output: 'standalone', } ``` **Step 2:** Use a multi-stage Dockerfile to build and run the app. (Next.js provides an official, highly optimized Dockerfile template on their GitHub repository). --- ## Production Readiness Checklist Before launching your app to real users, verify the following: - [ ] **Are Secrets Safe?** Ensure `NEXT_PUBLIC_` is NOT used on database strings or API secrets. - [ ] **Are Images Optimized?** Ensure you are using `next/image` instead of `` for large assets. - [ ] **Is LCP Optimized?** Add the `priority` prop to the main hero image on your landing page. - [ ] **Are Links Prefetching?** Ensure you are using the `` component instead of `` tags so Next.js can prefetch pages in the background. - [ ] **Are Layout Shifts Fixed?** Ensure all fonts and images have fallback dimensions to prevent layout shifting. - [ ] **Is Metadata Complete?** Ensure `title`, `description`, and `openGraph` tags are set in your root `layout.jsx`.

title: React Suspense and Streaming Architecture
summary: Master Streaming Server-Side Rendering (SSR) with React Suspense and loading.jsx to dramatically improve perceived performance and Time To First Byte (TTFB).
content:
## The Problem with Traditional SSR In traditional Server-Side Rendering (like Next.js Pages router or old Express apps), rendering is blocking. The server must: 1. Fetch ALL data for a page. 2. Render ALL HTML for the page. 3. Send ALL HTML to the client. If a page has a fast header, but a very slow database query for a data table, the user sees a blank white screen until the slow table query finishes. ## Enter Streaming and Suspense The Next.js App Router integrates deeply with React Suspense to enable **Streaming HTML**. Instead of waiting for all data, the server instantly streams the fast parts (the Header, the Sidebar) to the browser, and streams a placeholder (a skeleton loader) for the slow parts. When the slow database query finally finishes, the server streams the remaining HTML into the existing page. > **Definition: Streaming SSR** > Breaking down the HTML response into chunks and progressively sending them to the browser as soon as they are ready, rather than waiting for the entire page to finish rendering on the server. --- ## Using `loading.jsx` (Automatic Suspense) Next.js makes streaming incredibly easy. Simply create a `loading.jsx` file next to your `page.jsx`. Next.js will automatically wrap your `page.jsx` in a `` boundary using your `loading.jsx` as the fallback. ```jsx // src/app/dashboard/loading.jsx export default function DashboardLoading() { // This renders INSTANTLY while the page fetches data return
} ``` ```jsx // src/app/dashboard/page.jsx export default async function DashboardPage() { // Simulating a slow database query (3 seconds) await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 3000)) return

Dashboard Data Loaded!

} ``` Because of `loading.jsx`, the user sees the sidebar, navigation, and the skeleton loader instantly. Three seconds later, the skeleton loader is swapped out for the actual data. --- ## Granular Suspense (Manual Streaming) `loading.jsx` applies to the entire route. But what if your page has multiple independent slow components? You can manually wrap them in `` to stream them individually! ```jsx // src/app/analytics/page.jsx import { Suspense } from 'react' import RevenueChart from './RevenueChart' import UserTable from './UserTable' import Skeleton from '@/components/Skeleton' export default function AnalyticsPage() { return (

Analytics Dashboard

{/* The Revenue chart might take 2 seconds */} }> {/* The User table might take 5 seconds */} }>
) } ``` In the example above, the page shell loads instantly. The `RevenueChart` pops in after 2 seconds, and the `UserTable` pops in after 5 seconds. **No waterfall, and no blocked rendering.** > **Interview Highlight** > **Q: Explain how React Suspense improves Time To First Byte (TTFB).** > A: Without Suspense, the server holds the connection open and sends 0 bytes until the slowest data query finishes. With Suspense, the server immediately flushes the HTML for the static parts of the layout to the browser (drastically lowering TTFB), while suspending the slow components. It then streams the resolved HTML for the suspended components over the same connection when they finish.

title: In-Depth Caching in Next.js (The 4 Caches)
summary: Demystify Next.js aggressive caching mechanisms. Learn how Request Memoization, the Data Cache, the Full Route Cache, and the Router Cache work together.
content:
## The Next.js Caching Architecture Next.js 14+ is famously aggressive with caching. By default, it tries to cache as much as possible to improve performance and lower database costs. To truly master Next.js, you must understand its **4 Caching Mechanisms**. --- ## 1. Request Memoization (Server-Side) If you call `fetch()` with the exact same URL and options multiple times during the render of a single page, Next.js only executes the network request once. ```jsx // src/app/layout.jsx async function Layout() { const user = await fetch('https://api.myapp.com/me').then(r => r.json()) return
{user.name}
} // src/app/page.jsx async function Page() { // This does NOT hit the network again! It returns instantly from memory. const user = await fetch('https://api.myapp.com/me').then(r => r.json()) return

Welcome, {user.name}

} ``` **Lifespan:** Lasts only for the duration of a single server request. **Purpose:** Prevents prop-drilling. You can safely fetch data wherever you need it. --- ## 2. Data Cache (Server-Side) This caches the actual JSON data returned from external APIs across multiple user requests and deployments. ```jsx // Cached persistently across all users const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data') // Cached for 60 seconds (ISR) const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data', { next: { revalidate: 60 } }) // Bypasses the Data Cache entirely const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data', { cache: 'no-store' }) ``` **Lifespan:** Persistent across deployments until manually revalidated or cache-busted. **Purpose:** Speeds up external API calls and reduces load on third-party services. --- ## 3. Full Route Cache (Server-Side) This caches the fully rendered HTML and React Server Component (RSC) payload for a specific route. This is what makes Static Site Generation (SSG) work. If your route has no dynamic functions (like `cookies()`) and no uncached fetches, Next.js builds the HTML at compile time and stores it in the Full Route Cache. **Lifespan:** Persistent until you rebuild the app or manually trigger a revalidation (e.g., via `revalidatePath`). **Purpose:** Serves pages instantly from the edge CDN. --- ## 4. Router Cache (Client-Side) This is the only cache that lives in the user's browser. When a user navigates around your app using the `` component, Next.js caches the visited routes in the browser's memory. If they click "Back" or revisit a page they just saw, it loads instantly from the client's memory without hitting the server. ```jsx import Link from 'next/link' // Next.js prefetches this route in the background and stores it in the Router Cache About Us ``` **Lifespan:** Lasts for the duration of the user's session (until they hard refresh the browser window). **Purpose:** Makes client-side navigation feel instantaneous (SPA-like). --- > **Interview Highlight** > **Q: A user complains that after updating their profile, the dashboard still shows their old name, even though the database updated. Which caches could be responsible, and how do you fix it?** > A: This is likely an issue with the **Full Route Cache** or **Data Cache**. To fix it, you should call `revalidatePath('/dashboard')` inside the Server Action that updates the profile. This instantly purges the stale cache on the server, forcing Next.js to fetch the fresh data and rebuild the route.

title: Introduction to Node.js: What It Is, How It Works & When to Use It
summary: Understand what Node.js actually is under the hood — the V8 JavaScript engine, libuv, the single-threaded non-blocking I/O model, the Thread Pool, and when Node.js is the right (or wrong) tool for the job.
content: ## What is Node.js? — A True Definition

**Node.js** is an open-source, cross-platform **JavaScript runtime environment** built on Google Chrome's **V8 JavaScript engine**. Created by **Ryan Dahl in 2009**, Node.js lets you run JavaScript code _outside_ the browser — on servers, your local machine, IoT devices, and anywhere else.

Before Node.js, JavaScript was a browser-only language. Ryan Dahl saw that most web servers wasted time _waiting_ — waiting for a database query, waiting for a file to read, waiting for a network response. He built Node.js around a radically different idea: **never wait, never block**.
## The Three Pillars of Node.js Architecture

Node.js is built on three core layers that work together:

### 1. The V8 JavaScript Engine
V8 is Google's open-source JavaScript engine written in C++. It compiles JavaScript directly to optimised **native machine code** (not bytecode, not interpreted line-by-line). This is why Node.js is fast — your JS code runs almost as fast as C++.

### 2. Core Node.js APIs (C++ Bindings)
These are C++ modules that give your JavaScript code access to operating system features:
- File System (`fs`) — read/write files
- Network (`net`, `http`, `https`) — create servers and make requests
- Cryptography (`crypto`) — hashing and encryption
- Child Processes (`child_process`) — spawn OS commands

### 3. libuv — The Secret Weapon
**libuv** is a high-performance, multi-platform C library that handles **asynchronous I/O**. It provides:
- The **Event Loop** — the heart of Node.js
- A **Thread Pool** (default: 4 threads) for operations the OS can't handle asynchronously (file I/O, DNS lookups, crypto)
- Cross-platform abstractions for networking, timers, and signals
## Single-Threaded Non-Blocking I/O — How Node.js Handles 10,000 Concurrent Users

This is the most important concept to understand deeply.

**Traditional multi-threaded servers** (Apache, early Tomcat): Each request spawns a new thread. 10,000 users = 10,000 threads. Each thread uses ~1-2MB RAM = 10-20GB just for threads. Most threads just sit idle, _waiting_ for database results.

**Node.js single-threaded approach:**
1. Request arrives → Node reads it on the main thread (microseconds)
2. Needs DB query? → Offloads to the OS via libuv (Node's main thread is **free immediately**)
3. Main thread serves 9,999 other requests while DB query runs
4. DB query completes → OS notifies libuv → callback goes into the Event Queue
5. Event Loop picks up the callback → sends response

**The result:** Node can handle thousands of concurrent I/O-bound requests with minimal memory because threads aren't sitting idle waiting.
## Node.js vs. Browser JavaScript — Key Differences

| Feature | Browser JS | Node.js |
|---------|-----------|--------|
| `window` / `document` | ✅ Available | ❌ Does not exist |
| `process` object | ❌ | ✅ Provides env vars, args, exit |
| `require()` / `import` | Limited | ✅ Full module system |
| File System access | ❌ Sandboxed | ✅ Full `fs` module |
| `console.log()` | Writes to DevTools | Writes to stdout |
| Global object | `window` | `global` (or `globalThis`) |
| DOM APIs | ✅ | ❌ |
## When to Use Node.js (and When NOT To)

**Node.js excels at:**
- **REST and GraphQL APIs** — lightweight, fast, minimal overhead
- **Real-time applications** — chat apps, live dashboards, collaborative editors (using WebSockets)
- **Streaming** — Netflix, YouTube-like platforms that stream data in chunks
- **Microservices** — small, independently deployable services
- **CLI tools** — npm, webpack, ESLint, Prettier are all Node.js tools
- **BFF (Backend for Frontend)** — aggregate multiple APIs for a specific UI

**Node.js is a poor fit for:**
- **CPU-intensive tasks** — Video encoding, image processing, machine learning inference, heavy cryptography
- **Why?** These tasks cannot be offloaded to libuv's thread pool (it saturates quickly) and will **block the event loop**, freezing all other requests
- **Solution:** For CPU-intensive work, use Python, Go, Rust, or offload to worker threads / separate services
## Installing Node.js and Your First Server

Download Node.js from [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org). Always install the **LTS (Long Term Support)** version for production. Use **nvm** (Node Version Manager) to manage multiple versions on your machine.

title: The Node.js Event Loop: A Complete Visual Guide with Phases & Examples
summary: Deeply understand the Node.js Event Loop — all 6 phases (timers, pending callbacks, idle/prepare, poll, check, close), microtasks vs macrotasks, process.nextTick, queueMicrotask, and how to avoid blocking the loop.
content: ## What is the Node.js Event Loop?

The **Event Loop** is the mechanism that allows Node.js to perform non-blocking I/O operations despite JavaScript being single-threaded. It is implemented by **libuv** (not by the JavaScript engine itself) and is the core reason Node.js can handle thousands of concurrent connections.

Here is the simplest mental model:
> The Event Loop continuously checks: _'Is there any work to do?'_ If yes, it does it. If no, it waits. When an async operation finishes (e.g., a file was read, a timer fired, a DB query returned), it puts a callback into a queue. The Event Loop picks that callback up and runs it.
## The 6 Phases of the Event Loop

The Event Loop is not just a single queue — it runs through **6 ordered phases** in each 'tick' (iteration). Each phase has a FIFO queue of callbacks to execute.

### Phase 1: Timers
Executes callbacks scheduled by `setTimeout()` and `setInterval()`. The timer fires when the delay has expired AND the Event Loop reaches this phase. Note: a `setTimeout(fn, 0)` does NOT mean it runs immediately — it runs on the next Event Loop iteration at the earliest.

### Phase 2: Pending Callbacks
Executes I/O callbacks deferred to the next loop iteration (e.g., TCP errors, certain socket errors).

### Phase 3: Idle, Prepare
Used internally by libuv. You don't typically interact with this phase.

### Phase 4: Poll
This is the most important phase. It does two things:
1. Retrieves new I/O events and executes their callbacks (file reads, network data, database responses)
2. If no I/O is pending, it **waits here** for new I/O events (up to a calculated timeout)

If timers are scheduled, the Poll phase waits only long enough before transitioning to the Timers phase.

### Phase 5: Check (setImmediate)
Executes callbacks registered with `setImmediate()`. These run after the Poll phase completes.

### Phase 6: Close Callbacks
Executes close event callbacks (e.g., `socket.on('close', ...)`, `server.close()`).
## Microtasks vs Macrotasks — The Most Critical Distinction

**Between every phase** of the Event Loop, Node.js drains two special microtask queues:

1. **`process.nextTick()` queue** — runs FIRST, before anything else, including other microtasks
2. **Promise microtask queue** — runs second (resolved `.then()` callbacks, `await` continuations)

Microtasks always run **before** the next Event Loop phase. This means:
- A `process.nextTick()` callback runs before a `Promise.resolve().then()`
- Both run before `setImmediate()` or `setTimeout(fn, 0)`

**Macrotasks** (also called Task Queue): `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `setImmediate`, I/O callbacks — these all run in their respective Event Loop phases.
## setTimeout vs setImmediate vs process.nextTick — When Does Each Run?

This is the most common interview question about Node.js:

| API | When it runs | Phase |
|-----|-------------|-------|
| `process.nextTick(fn)` | Before next phase, before promises | Microtask Queue 1 |
| `Promise.resolve().then(fn)` | Before next phase, after nextTick | Microtask Queue 2 |
| `setImmediate(fn)` | In the Check phase, after current Poll phase | Phase 5 |
| `setTimeout(fn, 0)` | In the Timers phase, next iteration | Phase 1 |
| I/O callback | In the Poll phase | Phase 4 |

**Key insight:** Inside an I/O callback, `setImmediate` always runs before `setTimeout(fn, 0)` because the Poll phase runs before the Timers phase. Outside I/O callbacks, the order of `setImmediate` vs `setTimeout(fn, 0)` is non-deterministic.
## How to Avoid Blocking the Event Loop

**Blocking the Event Loop** means running synchronous, CPU-intensive code on the main thread for a long time. During this time, no other requests can be served — your server freezes.

**Common causes of blocking:**
- `JSON.parse()` / `JSON.stringify()` on huge payloads
- Synchronous `fs` methods (`readFileSync`, `writeFileSync`) in request handlers
- Complex regex operations on large strings
- Sorting or processing huge arrays synchronously

**Solutions:**
- Use async versions of everything
- Break heavy work into chunks using `setImmediate()` to yield to the Event Loop between chunks
- Use **Worker Threads** for truly CPU-intensive work
- Use clustering to run multiple Node.js processes

title: Node.js Core Modules Deep Dive: fs, path, os, events, http, crypto, url
summary: Master Node.js built-in core modules with real-world examples: fs (file system), path, os, EventEmitter, http, url, crypto, child_process, and util — no npm install needed.
content: ## What are Node.js Core Modules?

**Core modules** (also called built-in modules) are modules that ship with Node.js — no `npm install` required. They provide fundamental functionality like reading files, creating servers, emitting events, and accessing the operating system.

Import them using `require()` (CommonJS) or `import` (ES Modules):
```js
const fs = require('fs');          // CommonJS
import fs from 'fs';                // ES Modules (.mjs or type:module)
import { readFile } from 'fs/promises'; // Promise-based variant
```
## The `fs` Module — File System Operations

The `fs` module lets you interact with the file system. Always prefer the **Promise-based** API (`fs.promises` or `fs/promises`) over callbacks in modern Node.js.

**Reading files:** `readFile`, `readFileSync`
**Writing files:** `writeFile`, `appendFile`, `writeFileSync`
**File metadata:** `stat`, `access`, `exists`
**Directories:** `mkdir`, `rmdir`, `readdir`, `rm`
**File operations:** `copyFile`, `rename`, `unlink` (delete)
**Streaming:** `createReadStream`, `createWriteStream`
**Watching:** `watch`, `watchFile`
## The `path` Module — Cross-Platform File Paths

Always use the `path` module for file paths — never concatenate strings manually. Windows uses backslashes (`\`), Unix uses forward slashes (`/`). `path` handles this automatically.

`path.join(...segments)` — safely join path segments
`path.resolve(...segments)` — resolve to absolute path
`path.dirname(path)` — directory part
`path.basename(path, ext)` — filename part
`path.extname(path)` — file extension
`path.parse(path)` — break into { root, dir, base, ext, name }
`path.sep` — OS-specific separator (`/` or `\\`)

**`__dirname` and `__filename`:** In CommonJS, these give you the absolute path of the current file — essential for building paths relative to your source code.
## The `events` Module — EventEmitter

Node.js is built on an **event-driven architecture**. The `EventEmitter` class is the backbone of many Node.js core modules (`http.Server`, `fs.ReadStream`, `net.Socket` all extend it).

Key methods:
`emitter.on(event, listener)` — add persistent listener
`emitter.once(event, listener)` — add one-time listener
`emitter.emit(event, ...args)` — trigger event synchronously
`emitter.off(event, listener)` / `removeListener` — remove listener
`emitter.removeAllListeners(event)` — remove all
`emitter.listeners(event)` — get all listeners
`emitter.setMaxListeners(n)` — increase listener limit (default: 10)

**Memory leak warning:** Node.js warns you if you add more than 10 listeners to one event — this usually signals a missing `removeListener` in a loop.
## The `os` Module — Operating System Info

Useful for monitoring, health checks, and writing cross-platform code.

`os.cpus()` — array of CPU core info
`os.totalmem()` / `os.freemem()` — memory in bytes
`os.platform()` — 'linux', 'darwin', 'win32'
`os.arch()` — 'x64', 'arm64'
`os.hostname()` — machine hostname
`os.uptime()` — system uptime in seconds
`os.userInfo()` — current user info
`os.tmpdir()` — temp directory path
`os.EOL` — OS-specific line ending
## The `crypto` Module — Hashing, Encryption & Security

Never use external libraries for basic hashing — Node.js `crypto` handles it natively.

`crypto.randomBytes(n)` — cryptographically secure random bytes
`crypto.randomUUID()` — generate UUID v4 (Node 14.17+)
`crypto.createHash(algo)` — MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-512
`crypto.createHmac(algo, secret)` — HMAC for request signing
`crypto.pbkdf2Sync/Async` — password key derivation
`crypto.timingSafeEqual` — compare buffers without timing attacks
`crypto.createCipheriv/createDecipheriv` — AES encryption
## The `child_process` Module — Spawning Processes

Run shell commands, scripts, or other programs from Node.js.

`exec(command, callback)` — run shell command, buffer output (max 1MB)
`execFile(file, args, callback)` — run executable directly (safer, no shell)
`spawn(command, args, options)` — streaming I/O, for large outputs
`fork(modulePath)` — spawn a Node.js child process with IPC channel

title: Node.js Streams & Buffers: Process Gigabytes of Data Without Running Out of Memory
summary: Master Node.js Streams (Readable, Writable, Duplex, Transform) and Buffers. Learn how to process large files, HTTP request bodies, and data pipelines without loading everything into memory.
content: ## Why Streams? The Memory Problem

Imagine reading a 10GB log file without streams:
```js
const data = fs.readFileSync('./10gb-log.txt'); // CRASH — out of memory!
```

With streams, you process data in small **chunks** (typically 64KB) without ever holding the whole file in memory. This is how Node.js handles:
- Large file uploads and downloads
- HTTP request and response bodies
- Database result sets
- Video transcoding pipelines
- Real-time data processing
## What is a Buffer?

A **Buffer** is a fixed-size chunk of raw binary memory, allocated outside the V8 JavaScript heap. Buffers represent sequences of bytes (0-255). They are used when dealing with:
- Binary data (images, audio, video, compressed files)
- Network packets
- File I/O (files are binary, not JavaScript strings)
- Cryptographic operations

Buffers are a subclass of `Uint8Array` and have many of the same methods. In Node.js 10+, always use `Buffer.from()`, `Buffer.alloc()`, and `Buffer.allocUnsafe()` — never the deprecated `new Buffer()` constructor.
## The 4 Types of Streams

**1. Readable Stream** — source of data that you read FROM
- Examples: `fs.createReadStream()`, `http.IncomingMessage`, `process.stdin`, `crypto.randomBytes()` in streaming mode

**2. Writable Stream** — destination that you write TO
- Examples: `fs.createWriteStream()`, `http.ServerResponse`, `process.stdout`, `zlib.createGzip()`

**3. Duplex Stream** — both readable AND writable (independently)
- Examples: TCP sockets (`net.Socket`), WebSockets

**4. Transform Stream** — a Duplex stream where output is computed from input (data goes in, modified data comes out)
- Examples: `zlib.createGzip()` (compress), `zlib.createGunzip()` (decompress), `crypto.createCipheriv()`, custom CSV parsers
## Stream Modes: Flowing vs Paused

Readable streams have two modes:

**Paused mode (default):** Data sits in an internal buffer. You must explicitly call `.read()` or attach a `'data'` event listener to start consuming data.

**Flowing mode:** Data is pushed to you automatically as soon as it's available. Activated by `.pipe()`, `.resume()`, or adding a `'data'` event listener.

Best practice: Use `.pipe()` or the newer `stream.pipeline()` utility — they handle backpressure automatically.
## Backpressure — The Hidden Gotcha

**Backpressure** occurs when a Writable stream can't consume data as fast as a Readable stream produces it. Without handling it, Node.js buffers all the data in memory — causing memory leaks.

**Solution:** Use `pipe()` or `stream.pipeline()` — they automatically pause the Readable when the Writable's buffer is full, and resume when it drains.

If using `.write()` manually, always check its return value — it returns `false` when the buffer is full. Pause reading until the `'drain'` event fires.
## Custom Transform Streams

Transform streams are incredibly powerful for building data pipelines. You extend the `Transform` class and implement `_transform(chunk, encoding, callback)`. This is how tools like `csv-parser`, `JSONStream`, and compression libraries work internally.

title: Express.js Fundamentals: Routing, Request/Response, Template Engines & Project Structure
summary: Master Express.js from the ground up: installing and configuring Express, defining routes, working with request and response objects, serving static files, using template engines, and structuring a scalable project.
content: ## What is Express.js and Why Use It?

**Express.js** is a minimal, unopinionated web framework for Node.js. Without Express, you'd have to manually parse URLs, route requests, set headers, parse JSON bodies, and handle errors — all from scratch using Node's low-level `http` module. Express handles all of this, letting you focus on your application logic.

**Key features:**
- Clean, concise routing API (`app.get()`, `app.post()`, etc.)
- Powerful middleware system
- Template engine integration (EJS, Pug, Handlebars)
- Static file serving
- Robust error handling
- Massive ecosystem of third-party middleware
## Installing and Initializing Express

```bash
mkdir my-api && cd my-api
npm init -y
npm install express
npm install --save-dev nodemon  # auto-restart on file changes
```

Add to `package.json`:
```json
"scripts": {
  "dev": "nodemon src/index.js",
  "start": "node src/index.js"
}
```
## The Request Object (`req`) — Everything About the Incoming Request

`req.params` — URL parameters (e.g., `/users/:id` → `req.params.id`)
`req.query` — Query string (e.g., `/search?q=node` → `req.query.q`)
`req.body` — Request body (requires `express.json()` or `express.urlencoded()` middleware)
`req.headers` — Request headers
`req.method` — HTTP method ('GET', 'POST', etc.)
`req.url` — Full URL path
`req.path` — Path without query string
`req.hostname` — Request hostname
`req.ip` — Client IP address
`req.cookies` — Cookies (requires `cookie-parser` middleware)
`req.get(headerName)` — Get specific header
`req.is(type)` — Check Content-Type
## The Response Object (`res`) — Sending Responses

`res.send(body)` — Send any content (string, Buffer, object)
`res.json(obj)` — Send JSON (sets Content-Type automatically)
`res.status(code)` — Set HTTP status code (chainable)
`res.sendStatus(code)` — Set status + send status text
`res.redirect(url)` — Redirect to URL
`res.render(view, data)` — Render template engine view
`res.sendFile(path)` — Send a file
`res.download(path)` — Send file as attachment (triggers download)
`res.set(header, value)` — Set response header
`res.cookie(name, value, options)` — Set cookie
`res.clearCookie(name)` — Clear cookie
`res.end()` — End response without data
## Express Router — Organizing Routes

As your app grows, putting all routes in one file becomes unmanageable. Express's `Router` lets you split routes into separate modules by resource (users, posts, products). This is the foundation of the MVC architecture.
## Scalable Project Structure

The most battle-tested structure for Node.js + Express APIs:
```
src/
  index.js           — entry point, starts server
  app.js             — express setup, middleware, routes
  config/
    index.js         — environment variables and config
  routes/
    user.routes.js   — route definitions
    post.routes.js
  controllers/
    user.controller.js — request handlers
  services/
    user.service.js  — business logic
  models/
    User.js          — database models
  middlewares/
    auth.middleware.js
    error.middleware.js
  utils/
    logger.js
    helpers.js
```

title: Express Middleware: The Complete Guide — Built-in, Third-party & Custom Middleware
summary: Deeply understand Express middleware — the middleware pipeline, application-level vs router-level vs error-handling middleware, and building production-grade custom middleware for logging, rate limiting, authentication, and request validation.
content: ## What is Middleware? The Express Pipeline

**Middleware** is a function that has access to the request (`req`), the response (`res`), and the **next middleware function** in the pipeline (`next`). Every request in Express passes through a chain of middleware functions in the order they are defined.

Middleware can:
- Execute any code
- Modify `req` and `res` objects
- End the request-response cycle (`res.send()`, `res.json()`)
- Call `next()` to pass control to the next middleware
- Call `next(err)` to skip to the error handler

If middleware doesn't end the cycle OR call `next()`, the request **hangs** — it just times out.
## Types of Middleware

**1. Application-level middleware** — attached to the `app` instance with `app.use()` or `app.METHOD()`. Runs for every request (or a subset if a path is provided).

**2. Router-level middleware** — attached to a `Router` instance. Only runs for routes on that router.

**3. Error-handling middleware** — has **four** parameters `(err, req, res, next)` instead of three. MUST be defined last, after all other `app.use()` and route calls.

**4. Built-in middleware** — `express.json()`, `express.urlencoded()`, `express.static()`.

**5. Third-party middleware** — `cors`, `helmet`, `morgan`, `compression`, `cookie-parser`, `rate-limiter-flexible`, `multer`.
## Essential Third-Party Middleware Stack

Install them:
```bash
npm install cors helmet morgan compression cookie-parser express-rate-limit
```

- **`cors`** — handle CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) headers for browser requests
- **`helmet`** — sets security HTTP headers (Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, etc.)
- **`morgan`** — HTTP request logger with multiple formats (combined, dev, tiny)
- **`compression`** — gzip/brotli compress responses (saves 70-90% bandwidth)
- **`cookie-parser`** — parse Cookie headers into `req.cookies`
- **`express-rate-limit`** — rate limiting to prevent brute-force attacks
## Middleware Ordering — Critical!

Middleware is executed **in the exact order it's defined**. This matters enormously:

```js
// Correct order
app.use(helmet());             // 1. Security headers
app.use(cors(corsOptions));    // 2. CORS (before auth)
app.use(morgan('dev'));        // 3. Logging (before routes)
app.use(express.json());      // 4. Body parsing (before routes)
app.use(compression());       // 5. Compression
app.use('/api', router);      // 6. Routes
app.use(notFoundHandler);     // 7. 404 (after all routes)
app.use(globalErrorHandler);  // 8. Error handler (last!)
```
## Building Custom Middleware

Custom middleware is just a function `(req, res, next) => {}`. You can:
- Add properties to `req` for later middleware (e.g., `req.user = decodedToken`)
- Check conditions and reject requests early
- Measure response times
- Validate request bodies

Middleware is one of Express's most powerful patterns — master it and you master Express.

summary: Learn how to build a production-grade REST API following REST constraints and the MVC (Model-View-Controller) pattern, separating concerns into routes, controllers, services, and models for maximum scalability.
content: ## What is a REST API?

**REST (Representational State Transfer)** is an architectural style — not a protocol — for designing networked applications. A REST API is an API that follows REST constraints, using HTTP methods and URLs to represent resources and actions.

**6 REST Constraints:**
1. **Client-Server** — UI and data are separated
2. **Stateless** — each request contains all information needed; no session state on server
3. **Cacheable** — responses can be cached
4. **Uniform Interface** — consistent URL structure and HTTP methods
5. **Layered System** — client doesn't know if it's talking to end server or proxy
6. **Code on Demand (optional)** — server can send executable code
## RESTful URL Design — Best Practices

**Resources are nouns, not verbs:**
```
✅  GET /api/v1/users          — get all users
✅  GET /api/v1/users/123      — get user 123
✅  POST /api/v1/users         — create user
✅  PATCH /api/v1/users/123    — partial update user 123
✅  DELETE /api/v1/users/123   — delete user 123

❌  GET /api/v1/getUsers
❌  POST /api/v1/createUser
❌  GET /api/v1/deleteUser?id=123
```

**Nested resources:**
```
GET  /api/v1/posts/42/comments        — all comments on post 42
POST /api/v1/posts/42/comments        — add comment to post 42
DELETE /api/v1/posts/42/comments/7   — delete comment 7 from post 42
```

**Versioning:** Always version your API (`/api/v1/`). When you make breaking changes, add `/api/v2/` — existing clients won't break.
## HTTP Status Codes — The Right Code Matters

| Code | When to Use |
|------|------------|
| **200 OK** | Successful GET, PATCH, PUT |
| **201 Created** | Successful POST (new resource created) |
| **204 No Content** | Successful DELETE (no body to return) |
| **400 Bad Request** | Client sent malformed data or invalid input |
| **401 Unauthorized** | Not authenticated (no/invalid token) |
| **403 Forbidden** | Authenticated but not authorized (wrong role) |
| **404 Not Found** | Resource doesn't exist |
| **409 Conflict** | Duplicate resource (email already registered) |
| **422 Unprocessable Entity** | Validation errors (correct format, invalid data) |
| **429 Too Many Requests** | Rate limit exceeded |
| **500 Internal Server Error** | Unhandled server errors |
## MVC Architecture for Node.js APIs

**Model-View-Controller (MVC)** separates your application into three layers:

**Model** — data and business data rules (Mongoose schemas, database queries)
**View** — in APIs, this is your JSON response (no HTML views)
**Controller** — handles HTTP requests, calls services, sends responses

For Node.js APIs, we add a **Service layer** between Controller and Model:

```
HTTP Request
    ↓
 Router (defines URL patterns)
    ↓
 Controller (validate input, call service, format response)
    ↓
 Service (business logic, orchestration)
    ↓
 Model/Repository (database queries)
    ↓
 Database
```

**Why the Service layer?**
- Controllers should be thin — just HTTP concerns
- Services contain pure business logic
- Business logic can be reused across multiple controllers (HTTP + WebSocket + CLI)
- Services are easier to unit test (no HTTP concerns)
## Pagination, Filtering & Sorting

Any production API that returns lists needs pagination, filtering, and sorting. Never return unbounded lists — `GET /users` returning 10,000 rows will crash your frontend and exhaust your database.

**Cursor-based pagination** (best for large datasets): use the ID/timestamp of the last item as a cursor for the next page. Consistent even when new items are added.

**Offset-based pagination**: `?page=2&limit=20`. Simpler but inconsistent if data changes between pages.
