title: Modern JavaScript: ES6+ Features
summary: Deep dive into all modern JavaScript features from ES6 to ES2024: modules, destructuring, generators, iterators, Proxy, Reflect, symbols, tagged templates, and more.
content: ## The Evolution of JavaScript

ECMAScript 2015 (ES6) was a watershed moment — it introduced so many features that it changed how JavaScript is written. Every year since, new features have been added. Here we cover the most important modern JavaScript features you need to know.
## ES Modules (import/export)

Modules let you split code across multiple files and control what each file exports. **Named exports** — export specific named values. **Default export** — one primary export per file. **Re-exports** — `export { thing } from './module'`.

In the browser: `<script type='module'>`. In Node.js: use `.mjs` extension or `"type": "module"` in package.json.
## Destructuring
Already covered in Arrays and Objects chapters — but destructuring also works in function parameters, for...of loops, and can be combined with default values and renaming.
## Generators

A **generator function** (`function*`) can pause execution with `yield` and resume later. It returns a **generator object** which is both an iterator and iterable. Generators are powerful for creating lazy sequences, implementing iterators, and simplifying async code.
## Iterators & the Iterator Protocol

An **iterator** is an object with a `next()` method that returns `{ value, done }`. An **iterable** is an object with `[Symbol.iterator]()` that returns an iterator. The `for...of` loop works with any iterable. Built-in iterables: Arrays, Strings, Maps, Sets, arguments, NodeLists.
## Proxy & Reflect

**Proxy** wraps an object and intercepts fundamental operations (get, set, delete, etc.) with **handler traps**. Used for: validation, logging, reactive data systems (Vue 3 uses Proxy!), read-only objects.

**Reflect** provides the default behavior for all operations that Proxy can intercept.
## Symbols
Symbols are unique, immutable primitives. Well-known Symbols (like `Symbol.iterator`, `Symbol.toPrimitive`) customize built-in JavaScript behaviors.

title: DOM Manipulation
summary: Learn how the Document Object Model works and how to select, modify, create, and delete HTML elements dynamically using JavaScript. Master querySelector, innerHTML, classList, and more.
content: ## What is the DOM?

The **Document Object Model (DOM)** is a programming interface for HTML documents. When a browser loads an HTML page, it creates a tree-like structure of objects representing every element — called the **DOM tree**. JavaScript can read and modify this tree to dynamically change what the user sees without reloading the page.
## The document Object
`document` is the entry point to the DOM — it represents the entire HTML page. All DOM manipulation starts with `document`.
## Selecting Elements

`document.getElementById(id)` — single element by ID
`document.getElementsByClassName(name)` — live HTMLCollection
`document.getElementsByTagName(tag)` — live HTMLCollection
`document.querySelector(selector)` — first element matching CSS selector
`document.querySelectorAll(selector)` — NodeList of all matches
`element.closest(selector)` — nearest ancestor matching selector
`element.matches(selector)` — does element match?
## Reading & Modifying Content

`element.textContent` — text content (safe, no HTML parsing)
`element.innerHTML` — HTML as string (be careful with XSS!)
`element.outerHTML` — element including itself
`element.innerText` — visible text (respects CSS)
`element.value` — input field value
## Modifying Attributes & Styles

`element.setAttribute(name, value)` — set any attribute
`element.getAttribute(name)` — read attribute
`element.removeAttribute(name)` — remove attribute
`element.dataset.customKey` — access data-* attributes
`element.style.property` — inline CSS
`element.classList.add/remove/toggle/contains/replace` — class management
## Creating & Removing Elements

`document.createElement(tag)` — create new element
`document.createTextNode(text)` — create text node
`parent.appendChild(child)` — append to end
`parent.prepend(child)` — prepend to beginning
`parent.insertBefore(newEl, refEl)` — insert before reference
`element.insertAdjacentHTML(position, html)` — fast HTML insertion
`element.remove()` — remove from DOM
`parent.removeChild(child)` — remove child

title: JavaScript Events
summary: Master JavaScript event handling: addEventListener, event bubbling, capturing, delegation, common events (click, input, keyboard, form, mouse), and custom events.
content: ## What is an Event?

An **event** is a signal that something has happened in the browser — a user click, a key press, a page load, a form submission, a mouse movement. JavaScript can **listen** for these events and respond with a callback function called an **event handler** or **event listener**.
## addEventListener

`element.addEventListener(type, handler, options)` — the modern way to attach event listeners. You can attach **multiple** listeners for the same event, and easily remove them with `removeEventListener`.
## The Event Object

Every event handler receives an **event object** (usually named `e` or `event`) with information about the event:

`event.type` — event type ('click', 'keydown')
`event.target` — element that triggered the event
`event.currentTarget` — element the listener is attached to
`event.preventDefault()` — prevent default browser behavior
`event.stopPropagation()` — stop event from bubbling up
`event.stopImmediatePropagation()` — stop bubbling AND other same-element listeners
## Event Bubbling & Capturing

When an event fires, it goes through **three phases**:
1. **Capture phase** — event travels from window down to target
2. **Target phase** — event is at the target element
3. **Bubble phase** — event travels back up from target to window

By default, listeners run in the **bubble** phase. Pass `{ capture: true }` to run in capture phase.
## Event Delegation

Instead of attaching listeners to every child element, attach ONE listener to a **parent**. Use `event.target` to determine which child was clicked. Much more efficient — works for dynamically added elements too!
## Common Events

**Mouse**: `click`, `dblclick`, `mousedown`, `mouseup`, `mousemove`, `mouseenter`, `mouseleave`, `mouseover`, `mouseout`, `contextmenu`
**Keyboard**: `keydown`, `keyup`, `keypress` (deprecated)
**Form**: `submit`, `change`, `input`, `focus`, `blur`, `reset`
**Window**: `load`, `DOMContentLoaded`, `resize`, `scroll`, `beforeunload`
**Clipboard**: `cut`, `copy`, `paste`
**Drag**: `dragstart`, `drag`, `dragenter`, `dragover`, `dragleave`, `drop`
**Touch**: `touchstart`, `touchmove`, `touchend`
**Media**: `play`, `pause`, `ended`, `timeupdate`

title: JSON & Web Storage APIs
summary: Master JSON parsing and serialization, localStorage, sessionStorage, cookies, and IndexedDB — learn how to persist data in the browser effectively and securely.
content: ## What is JSON?

**JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)** is a lightweight, text-based data interchange format. It's human-readable and language-independent. JSON is the de facto standard for APIs and data exchange on the web. JSON is NOT JavaScript — it's a string format that looks like JavaScript object literals.
## JSON vs JavaScript

Key differences from JS object literals:
- **Keys must be double-quoted strings** — `{"name": "Alice"}`, not `{name: 'Alice'}`
- **No functions, symbols, or undefined** — these don't serialize
- **No comments** allowed
- **No trailing commas**
- Valid JSON values: string, number, boolean, null, array, object
## JSON Methods

`JSON.parse(jsonString)` — parse a JSON string into a JavaScript value
`JSON.stringify(value, replacer, space)` — convert a JS value to JSON string

**Replacer** — array of keys to include, or a function to transform values
**Space** — indent for pretty-printing (number or string)
## localStorage

`localStorage` persists data with **no expiration** — survives browser restarts. Stores string key-value pairs. Max ~5MB.

`localStorage.setItem(key, value)` — store (converts to string!)
`localStorage.getItem(key)` — retrieve (or null)
`localStorage.removeItem(key)` — delete one
`localStorage.clear()` — delete all
`localStorage.length` — number of stored items
`localStorage.key(index)` — get key by index
## sessionStorage
Same API as `localStorage` but data is cleared when the **browser tab is closed**. Useful for temporary session data.
## Cookies

Cookies are older, more complex. They can be set to expire, sent to the server with every request, restricted by domain/path, and marked as HttpOnly (JS can't read). For client-only storage, prefer localStorage. For auth tokens, use HttpOnly cookies.

title: Regular Expressions (RegEx)
summary: Master JavaScript Regular Expressions: creating patterns, character classes, quantifiers, groups, flags, lookahead/lookbehind, and practical use cases for validation, search, and replacement.
content: ## What is a Regular Expression?

A **Regular Expression (RegEx)** is a sequence of characters that defines a search pattern. They are used for:
- **Validating** input (email, phone, URL)
- **Searching** for patterns in text
- **Extracting** specific parts of strings
- **Replacing** text based on patterns
## Creating Regular Expressions

**Literal syntax**: `/pattern/flags` — preferred, compiled at load time
**Constructor**: `new RegExp('pattern', 'flags')` — useful when pattern comes from a variable
## Flags

`g` — global: find ALL matches (not just first)
`i` — case insensitive
`m` — multiline: `^` and `$` match start/end of each LINE
`s` — dotAll: `.` matches newlines too
`u` — unicode: full Unicode support
`d` — indices: include match indices in results (ES2022)
## Character Classes

`.` — any character (except newline without `s` flag)
`\d` — digit `[0-9]`
`\D` — non-digit
`\w` — word char `[a-zA-Z0-9_]`
`\W` — non-word char
`\s` — whitespace (space, tab, newline)
`\S` — non-whitespace
`[abc]` — any of a, b, c
`[^abc]` — not a, b, c
`[a-z]` — range a to z
## Quantifiers

`*` — 0 or more
`+` — 1 or more
`?` — 0 or 1 (optional)
`{n}` — exactly n
`{n,}` — n or more
`{n,m}` — between n and m

Add `?` after quantifier for **lazy** (non-greedy) matching: `*?`, `+?`
## Anchors & Boundaries

`^` — start of string (or line in multiline mode)
`$` — end of string
`\b` — word boundary
`\B` — non-word boundary
## Groups & Lookaheads

`(abc)` — capturing group — captured in match
`(?:abc)` — non-capturing group — groups without capturing
`(?<name>abc)` — named capturing group (ES2018)
`(?=abc)` — positive lookahead — must be followed by 'abc'
`(?!abc)` — negative lookahead
`(?<=abc)` — positive lookbehind — must be preceded by 'abc'
`(?<!abc)` — negative lookbehind

content: ## The Number Type

JavaScript has a single numeric type — `Number` — which uses 64-bit IEEE 754 double-precision floating point. This means integers up to 2^53-1 are safe, and floating point math can have precision issues (`0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3`).
## Number Methods & Properties

`Number.isInteger(n)` — check if integer
`Number.isFinite(n)` — check if finite
`Number.isNaN(n)` — reliable NaN check (unlike global `isNaN`)
`Number.isSafeInteger(n)` — within safe integer range
`Number.parseInt(str, radix)` — same as global parseInt
`Number.parseFloat(str)` — same as global parseFloat
`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` — 9007199254740991 (2^53-1)
`Number.MIN_SAFE_INTEGER` — -9007199254740991
`Number.EPSILON` — smallest difference between floats
`Number.MAX_VALUE` — largest representable number

Instance methods:
`.toFixed(n)` — fixed decimal places (returns string)
`.toPrecision(n)` — significant digits
`.toString(radix)` — convert to different base (binary, hex, etc.)
`.toLocaleString()` — format per locale
## The Math Object

`Math.abs(n)` — absolute value
`Math.ceil(n)` — round up
`Math.floor(n)` — round down
`Math.round(n)` — round to nearest
`Math.trunc(n)` — remove decimal part
`Math.max(...args)` — largest value
`Math.min(...args)` — smallest value
`Math.random()` — random 0-1
`Math.pow(base, exp)` — power (prefer `**` operator)
`Math.sqrt(n)` — square root
`Math.cbrt(n)` — cube root
`Math.hypot(...args)` — hypotenuse
`Math.log(n)` — natural log
`Math.log2(n)` — log base 2
`Math.log10(n)` — log base 10
`Math.sin/cos/tan` — trig functions (radians)
`Math.PI` — 3.14159...
`Math.E` — Euler's number
`Math.sign(n)` — -1, 0, or 1
`Math.clz32(n)` — leading zeros in 32-bit representation
## The Date Object

`new Date()` — current date/time
`new Date(timestamp)` — from milliseconds since epoch
`new Date(dateString)` — from string (ISO 8601 recommended)
`new Date(year, month, day, h, m, s, ms)` — from parts (month is 0-indexed!)
`Date.now()` — current timestamp in ms (most efficient)
`Date.parse(str)` — parse string to timestamp
## Date Methods

**Getters**: `.getFullYear()`, `.getMonth()` (0-11!), `.getDate()` (day of month), `.getDay()` (day of week, 0=Sun), `.getHours()`, `.getMinutes()`, `.getSeconds()`, `.getMilliseconds()`, `.getTime()` (timestamp)

**Setters**: `.setFullYear()`, `.setMonth()`, `.setDate()`, `.setHours()`, etc.

**Formatting**: `.toISOString()`, `.toLocaleDateString()`, `.toLocaleTimeString()`, `.toLocaleString()`

title: JavaScript Best Practices & Design Patterns
summary: Learn JavaScript best practices, coding conventions, performance optimizations, common design patterns (Module, Observer, Factory, Singleton), and how to write clean, maintainable JavaScript.
content: ## Why Best Practices Matter

Writing code that works is just the beginning. Professional JavaScript requires code that is **readable**, **maintainable**, **performant**, and **bug-resistant**. Best practices are lessons learned by the community through real-world experience.
## Code Quality

- **Use `const` by default**, `let` when you need to reassign, never `var`
- **Use strict equality** (`===`) not loose (`==`)
- **Prefer arrow functions** for callbacks and short functions
- **Use template literals** over string concatenation
- **Use optional chaining** (`?.`) and nullish coalescing (`??`) to handle null/undefined
- **Always handle Promises** — never ignore `.catch()` or lack try/catch in async functions
- **Keep functions small** — Single Responsibility Principle
- **Use descriptive names** — `getUserById` not `getU`, `isLoggedIn` not `flag`
## Performance Optimizations

- **Debounce** expensive event handlers (search, resize, scroll)
- **Throttle** rate-limited functions
- **Use DocumentFragment** for batch DOM insertions
- **Avoid layout thrashing** — batch DOM reads and writes
- **Lazy load** modules with dynamic `import()`
- **Cache DOM queries** — don't query the DOM inside loops
- **Prefer `Map`/`Set`** over objects for frequent lookups
## Common Design Patterns

**Module Pattern** — encapsulate private state and expose a public API
**Factory Pattern** — functions that create and return objects
**Singleton Pattern** — ensure only one instance exists
**Observer/EventEmitter** — subscribe/publish pattern for decoupled components
**Strategy Pattern** — encapsulate algorithms behind a common interface
**Command Pattern** — encapsulate operations as objects (supports undo)
## Debugging Tips

- `console.log` with labels: `console.log('user:', user)` not just `console.log(user)`
- `console.table(array)` — display arrays/objects as a table
- `console.group(label)` / `console.groupEnd()` — group related logs
- `console.time(label)` / `console.timeEnd(label)` — measure performance
- `debugger;` — set a breakpoint in code
- Browser DevTools: Breakpoints, Network tab, Performance profiler

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to HTML & The Anatomy of a Web Page
summary: Learn the foundational structure of every web page. We cover the document structure, DOCTYPE declaration, the html root element, the head (metadata), and the body (visible content).
content: ## What is HTML?

**HTML (HyperText Markup Language)** is the standard markup language used to create and structure pages on the World Wide Web. It is not a programming language; it is a *markup* language that tells the web browser how to display text, images, and other multimedia.

- **HyperText:** Refers to links that connect web pages to one another.
- **Markup Language:** Uses "tags" to annotate text, defining how it should be structured or presented.
## The Anatomy of an HTML Element

Most HTML elements consist of an **opening tag**, the **content**, and a **closing tag**. ```html Content goes here ``` - **Opening tag:** The name of the element enclosed in angle brackets (e.g., `

`). - **Closing tag:** Identical to the opening tag, but with a forward slash before the name (e.g., `

`). - **Attributes:** Provide additional information about elements. Always specified in the opening tag. *Note: Some elements are "empty" or "void" elements and do not have a closing tag (e.g., `
`, ``, ``, ``).*
## The Essential HTML Document Structure
Every valid HTML5 document follows a strict baseline structure.
### 1. The `<!DOCTYPE html>` Declaration
This must be the very first line of your document. It tells the web browser that this page is written in HTML5. Without it, browsers might render the page in "quirks mode," breaking modern styling.
### 2. The `<html>` Root Element

The `<html>` tag wraps all the content on the entire page and is known as the root element. It is highly recommended to include the `lang` attribute (e.g., `lang="en"`) to declare the language of the page, which is crucial for accessibility (screen readers) and SEO.
### 3. The `<head>` Element (Metadata)

The `<head>` acts as a container for metadata (data about data). Nothing inside the `<head>` is directly displayed on the web page itself (except the `<title>`).

Inside the head, you will typically find:
- `<meta charset="UTF-8">`: Sets the character encoding to UTF-8, ensuring all international characters, symbols, and emojis display correctly.
- `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">`: Absolutely necessary for mobile-responsive design. It tells the browser to match the screen's width.
- `<title>`: Sets the title of the page, which appears in the browser tab and Google search results. This is the single most important SEO element on a page.
- `<link>` and `<style>` tags to connect CSS.
- `<script>` tags to load JavaScript.
### 4. The `<body>` Element (Visible Content)
The `<body>` contains all the content that users actually see on the screen—text, images, links, tables, lists, etc. There can only be one `<body>` element in an HTML document.

summary: Master all HTML text formatting tags. From headings (h1-h6) and paragraphs to structural tags like div/span and semantic formatting tags like strong, em, blockquote, and code.
content: ## Block-level vs Inline Elements

Before styling text, you must understand the difference between block and inline elements: - **Block-level elements** always start on a new line and take up the full width available (stretching left to right). Examples: `

` to `

`, `

`, `

`. - **Inline elements** do not start on a new line and only take up as much width as necessary. Examples: ``, ``, ``.
## Headings: `<h1>` to `<h6>`

Headings are used to define the hierarchical structure of a page. `<h1>` is the most important (the main title), and `<h6>` is the least important.

**SEO & Accessibility Rule:** You should only ever have **one** `<h1>` per page. Do not skip heading levels (e.g., jumping from `<h2>` directly to `<h4>`).
## Paragraphs and Line Breaks

The `

` tag defines a paragraph. Browsers automatically add margin (empty space) before and after a paragraph. The `
` (line break) tag forces a line break without starting a new paragraph. It is an empty/void element (no closing tag). *Note: Do not use `
` to create visual space between elements; use CSS margins instead.*
## The `<div>` and `<span>` Tags

These are generic containers with no inherent semantic meaning. They are primarily used to group elements together for styling with CSS or manipulation with JavaScript.
- `<div>`: A generic block-level container.
- `<span>`: A generic inline container (used to style a specific word inside a paragraph).
## Semantic Text Formatting Tags

In modern HTML, you should use tags that describe the *meaning* of the text, rather than how it looks. Screen readers use these to change voice inflection.

- `<strong>`: Defines text with strong importance (usually rendered as bold).
- `<em>`: Defines emphasized text (usually rendered as italic).
- `<b>`: Bold text (use only if `<strong>` is not appropriate semantically).
- `<i>`: Italic text (used for technical terms, foreign words).
- `<mark>`: Highlighted text (rendered with a yellow background).
- `<del>`: Deleted text (rendered with a strikethrough).
- `<ins>`: Inserted text (rendered with an underline).
- `<sub>`: Subscript text (appears half a character below the line, e.g., H₂O).
- `<sup>`: Superscript text (appears half a character above the line, e.g., E = mc²).
## Quotations and Code

HTML provides specific tags for quoting sources and writing code:
- `<blockquote>`: For long, block-level quotations from another source. Browsers typically indent it.
- `<q>`: For short, inline quotations. Browsers automatically insert quotation marks.
- `<cite>`: Defines the title of a creative work (a book, a poem, a movie).
- `<code>`: Defines a snippet of computer code (rendered in a monospace font).
- `<pre>`: Preformatted text. Preserves both spaces and line breaks exactly as they are written in the HTML file.

title: Chapter 3: HTML Links, Anchors, and Navigation Paths
summary: Dive deep into the anchor <a> tag. Learn how to link to external websites, link between pages on your own site using relative paths, create email/phone links, and jump to specific sections using ID anchors.
content: ## The Anchor Tag `<a>`

Links are the defining feature of the World Wide Web. They are created using the `<a>` (anchor) tag. The most important attribute of the `<a>` tag is the `href` (Hypertext REFerence) attribute, which indicates the link's destination.
## Absolute vs. Relative URLs

**Absolute URLs** include the full web address (e.g., `https://www.google.com`). They are used to link to external websites.

**Relative URLs** point to a file within the same website. They do not include the domain name. Understanding relative paths is crucial for building multi-page websites:
- `about.html`: Links to a file in the exact same folder.
- `images/logo.png`: Links to a file inside a subfolder named 'images'.
- `../contact.html`: Links to a file in the parent directory (one folder up).
## The `target` Attribute

By default, clicking a link opens the new page in the current browser tab. The `target` attribute specifies where to open the linked document.

- `target="_self"`: Default behavior. Opens in the same window/tab.
- `target="_blank"`: Opens the linked document in a new window or tab. *Security tip: When using `_blank` for external sites, it was historically recommended to add `rel="noopener noreferrer"` to prevent the new page from having control over the original page, though modern browsers now do this automatically.*
## Anchor Links (Jumping to a section on the same page)

You can link to a specific part of a web page using an ID. This is widely used for "Back to Top" buttons or Tables of Contents. 1. Give the target element a unique `id` attribute (e.g., `

Pricing

`). 2. Create a link with the `href` pointing to that ID with a hash symbol (e.g., `Go to Pricing`).
## Special Links: Mailto and Tel
You can create links that trigger the user's default email client or phone dialer. - **Email:** `Email Us` - **Phone:** `Call Us`

title: Chapter 4: HTML Images, Picture Element & Multimedia (Audio/Video)
summary: Learn how to embed media in your web pages. We cover the img tag and its crucial attributes (src, alt, loading), responsive images using the picture tag, embedding audio and video players, and using iframes for YouTube embeds.
content: ## The `` Tag

Images are not technically inserted into a web page; they are linked to it. The `` tag creates a holding space for the referenced image. It is an empty tag (no closing tag). **Required Attributes:** - `src` (Source): The path or URL to the image file. - `alt` (Alternate Text): A text description of the image. This is **mandatory** for accessibility (screen readers) and SEO. It also displays if the image fails to load.
## Best Practices for Images

1. **Always specify width and height:** Adding `width` and `height` attributes prevents "Cumulative Layout Shift" (CLS), a frustrating experience where text jumps around as images load.
2. **Lazy Loading:** Add `loading="lazy"` to images that are below the fold (not immediately visible when the page loads). The browser will only download them when the user scrolls near them, vastly improving page load speed.
## The `<picture>` Element (Art Direction)

The `` tag is a powerful element that allows you to display different images based on the user's screen size or device capabilities (like WebP support). This is crucial for responsive design. It contains one or more `` tags and one `` tag as a fallback.
## Embedding Audio

The `<audio>` tag allows you to embed sound content. The `controls` attribute adds play, pause, and volume controls. You can provide multiple `<source>` files (like .mp3 and .ogg) to ensure cross-browser compatibility.
## Embedding Video

The `<video>` tag works exactly like the audio tag. It supports attributes like `controls`, `autoplay`, `loop`, and `muted`. 
*Note: Most modern browsers block `autoplay` on videos that have sound. If you want a video to autoplay as a background, you MUST include the `muted` attribute.*
## The `<iframe>` Tag
An iframe (inline frame) is used to embed another document within the current HTML document. It is most commonly used to embed YouTube videos, Google Maps, or third-party widgets.

title: Chapter 5: HTML Lists — Unordered, Ordered, and Definition Lists
summary: Organize your content effectively using the three types of HTML lists. Learn how to create bulleted lists, numbered lists, description lists, and how to nest them for complex data.
content: ## Unordered Lists `<ul>`

An unordered list is used to group a set of related items in no particular order. By default, it is rendered with bullet points.
- The `<ul>` tag defines the unordered list.
- The `<li>` (list item) tag is used for each item inside the list.
## Ordered Lists `<ol>`

An ordered list is used when the sequence of items is important (e.g., a recipe or a top 10 list). By default, it is rendered with numbers.
- The `<ol>` tag defines the ordered list.
- The `<li>` tag is used for each item.

**Attributes for `<ol>`:**
- `type`: Changes the numbering style (`1` for numbers, `A` for uppercase letters, `a` for lowercase letters, `I` for roman numerals).
- `start`: Defines the starting number of the list.
- `reversed`: Reverses the numbering order (e.g., 3, 2, 1).
## Description Lists `<dl>`

A description list (or definition list) is used to display name/value pairs, such as terms and their definitions.
- `<dl>`: Defines the description list.
- `<dt>`: Defines the term (name).
- `<dd>`: Defines the description (value) for the preceding term.
## Nesting Lists

You can place lists inside of other lists. This is called nesting. It is essential for creating multi-level navigation menus and complex outlines. *Important rule: The nested `<ul>` or `<ol>` must be placed INSIDE an `<li>` element, not directly inside the parent `<ul>`.*

title: Chapter 6: HTML Tables — Structuring Tabular Data
summary: Master the creation of data tables. Learn the core table tags, how to define headers, group rows into semantic sections (thead, tbody, tfoot), and merge cells using colspan and rowspan.
content: ## The Basics of HTML Tables
Tables are used exclusively for displaying tabular data (data that makes sense in a grid of rows and columns, like a spreadsheet). *Do not use tables for page layout.*

**Core Table Tags:**
- `<table>`: The container for the entire table.
- `<tr>` (Table Row): Defines a horizontal row of cells.
- `<th>` (Table Header): Defines a header cell (automatically bold and centered).
- `<td>` (Table Data): Defines a standard data cell.
## Semantic Table Sections

For complex tables, it is best practice to divide the table into semantic sections. This helps screen readers, allows for specific CSS targeting, and enables scrolling bodies with fixed headers.

- `<thead>`: Groups the header content.
- `<tbody>`: Groups the main body content.
- `<tfoot>`: Groups the footer content (e.g., totals or summaries).
- `<caption>`: Provides a title/caption for the table (must be the first child of `<table>`).
## Spanning Rows and Columns

Sometimes a single cell needs to stretch across multiple columns or multiple rows.
- `colspan="number"`: Stretches a cell horizontally across multiple columns.
- `rowspan="number"`: Stretches a cell vertically across multiple rows.
## The `<colgroup>` and `<col>` Tags
These tags allow you to apply styles to entire columns at once, rather than adding a class to every single `<td>` in that column.

title: Chapter 7: HTML Forms — Collecting User Input (Part 1)
summary: Forms are the primary way users interact with a web application. Learn how to create forms, use the versatile <input> tag, understand the difference between GET and POST, and bind inputs to labels for accessibility.
content: ## The `<form>` Tag

The `<form>` element acts as a container for all input controls. It tells the browser where to send the data and how to send it.

**Crucial Attributes:**
- `action`: The URL where the form data should be sent when submitted (e.g., `/api/login`).
- `method`: The HTTP method used to send the data.
  - `GET`: Appends the data to the URL (e.g., `?search=shoes`). Used for retrieving data (searches, filters). Never use for sensitive data.
  - `POST`: Sends the data in the HTTP request body. Used for submitting data (login, registration, payments).
- `enctype`: Specifies how data should be encoded. Usually left default, but MUST be set to `multipart/form-data` if the form includes file uploads.
## The `<input>` Element and `type`

The `<input>` tag is the most versatile element in HTML. It is an empty tag. Its behavior changes entirely based on the `type` attribute.

**Common Text Inputs:**
- `type="text"`: Standard single-line text field.
- `type="password"`: Masks the characters as dots or asterisks.
- `type="email"`: On mobile, brings up a keyboard with an '@' symbol. Automatically validates for an email format.
- `type="number"`: Ensures only numbers are entered, usually adds up/down arrows.
- `type="search"`, `type="tel"`, `type="url"`: Semantic variations of text inputs.
## The `name` and `value` Attributes

- `name`: **Extremely important.** When the form is submitted, the data is sent as name/value pairs. Without a `name` attribute, the input's data will NOT be sent to the server.
- `value`: Specifies the initial or default value of the input.
## The `<label>` Element

A `<label>` describes what an input is for. It is critical for accessibility (screen readers). Furthermore, clicking the label text will automatically focus the associated input or toggle the checkbox.

To bind a label to an input, the `for` attribute of the label MUST exactly match the `id` attribute of the input.
## Checkboxes and Radio Buttons

- `type="radio"`: Allows selecting **only one** option from a group. To group radio buttons together, they must all share the exact same `name` attribute.
- `type="checkbox"`: Allows selecting **multiple** options from a group.

title: Chapter 8: HTML Forms — Advanced Controls, Selects, and Textareas
summary: Move beyond the basic <input> tag. Learn how to create dropdown menus, multi-line text areas, group form elements visually with fieldsets, and use HTML5 validation attributes.
content: ## Dropdown Menus: `<select>` and `<option>`

When you have many options but want to save space, use a dropdown menu.
- `<select>`: Creates the dropdown container. This element receives the `name` attribute.
- `<option>`: Defines an individual item in the list. This receives the `value` attribute.
- `<optgroup>`: Allows you to group related `<option>` elements under a non-selectable header.
## Multi-line Text: `<textarea>`

The `<input type="text">` tag is only for a single line of text. For paragraphs, comments, or messages, use `<textarea>`.

Unlike `<input>`, `<textarea>` has a closing tag. Any text placed between the opening and closing tags becomes the default value. You can control its initial size using the `rows` and `cols` attributes.
## The `<button>` Element

While you can use `<input type="submit">`, the `<button>` element is much more versatile because it is a container tag. You can put icons, images, or strong text inside a `<button>`, which you cannot do with an `<input>`.

**Button Types:**
- `type="submit"`: (Default inside a form) Submits the form.
- `type="button"`: Does nothing by default. Used to trigger JavaScript functions.
- `type="reset"`: Resets all form inputs to their initial values.
## Grouping Elements: `<fieldset>` and `<legend>`
To logically and visually group related form controls together (e.g., grouping all shipping address fields together), use `<fieldset>`. The `<legend>` element provides a caption for the fieldset.
## HTML5 Input Types and Validation

HTML5 introduced powerful native validation and new input types:
- `type="color"`: Opens a color picker.
- `type="date"`, `type="time"`: Opens a calendar/clock picker.
- `type="range"`: Creates a slider.
- `type="file"`: Allows users to upload files.

**Validation Attributes:**
- `required`: The form cannot be submitted if this field is empty.
- `min` / `max`: For numbers and dates.
- `maxlength` / `minlength`: For text strings.
- `pattern`: Validates the input against a Regular Expression.

title: Chapter 9: Semantic HTML5 — Writing Meaningful Markup
summary: Stop using <div> for everything! Learn the HTML5 semantic tags that describe the meaning of your content, drastically improving your site's SEO, accessibility, and code readability.
content: ## What is Semantic HTML?

Semantic HTML refers to tags that provide meaning to the web page rather than just presentation. 

Before HTML5, developers built layouts using `<div id="header">`, `<div class="nav">`, and `<div id="footer">`. While visually fine, search engines and screen readers had no idea what those `<div>`s actually contained because `<div>` is semantically meaningless.
## The Core HTML5 Semantic Tags

HTML5 introduced tags that explicitly describe their role in the document structure:

- `<header>`: The introductory content of a page or section (usually contains the logo and main heading).
- `<nav>`: The primary navigation links of the site.
- `<main>`: The dominant, unique content of the page. There should only be one `<main>` tag per page.
- `<article>`: A self-contained, independent piece of content (like a blog post, news story, or forum post) that makes sense on its own.
- `<section>`: A thematic grouping of content, typically with its own heading.
- `<aside>`: Content that is tangentially related to the main content (like a sidebar, glossary, or related links).
- `<footer>`: The closing content of a page or section (copyright info, secondary links).
## Images and Figures
Instead of just using ``, HTML5 gives us a semantic way to group an image with its caption: - `
## Time and Details

- `<time>`: Used to represent a specific period in time or a date. It includes a `datetime` attribute that is machine-readable by search engines.
- `<details>` and `<summary>`: Creates a native, interactive "accordion" or "dropdown" widget without any JavaScript! The `<summary>` is the clickable heading, and the content inside `<details>` expands when clicked.

title: Chapter 10: HTML Meta Tags & SEO Best Practices
summary: Master the <head> element. Learn how to write SEO-optimized titles and descriptions, configure the viewport for mobile devices, use Canonical links, and add Open Graph tags for beautiful social media sharing.
content: ## The Importance of the `<head>`

The `<head>` section is where you configure metadata. While this content isn't visible on the page itself, it dictates how search engines (Google), social media platforms (Twitter, Facebook), and browsers interpret and display your site.
## Essential SEO Meta Tags

- `<title>`: The most important SEO factor. Keep it between 50-60 characters. Place your primary keyword near the beginning.
- `<meta name="description">`: A summary of the page (150-160 characters). Google often uses this as the snippet below the title in search results. It doesn't directly impact ranking, but heavily influences Click-Through Rate (CTR).
## The Viewport Meta Tag

Without this tag, mobile browsers will assume your page is designed for desktop (around 980px wide) and zoom out, making the text tiny and unreadable.

`<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">` tells the browser to match the screen's width and set the initial zoom to 100%.
## Open Graph & Twitter Cards

When you share a link on iMessage, Slack, Twitter, or Facebook, a beautiful card with an image, title, and description appears. This is achieved using Open Graph (`og:`) and Twitter (`twitter:`) meta tags.
## Canonical Links and Favicons

Using the `<link>` tag:
- **Favicon:** The small icon in the browser tab. `<link rel="icon" href="favicon.ico">`
- **Canonical URL:** If you have duplicate content on different URLs (e.g., `example.com/shoes` and `example.com/shoes?sort=price`), the canonical link tells Google which URL is the "master" version to index, preventing duplicate content penalties.

    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    
    <!-- Primary SEO -->

    <meta name="description" content="Order locally grown, 100% organic apples delivered straight to your door. Crisp, sweet, and pesticide-free.">
    <meta name="keywords" content="organic apples, fruit delivery, local farm"> <!-- Note: Google ignores keywords now -->
    
    <!-- Canonical Link -->

    <!-- Favicon -->
    <link rel="icon" type="image/png" href="/images/favicon.png">
    
    <!-- Open Graph (Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack, iMessage) -->
    <meta property="og:title" content="Buy Fresh Organic Apples">
    <meta property="og:description" content="Delivered straight to your door within 24 hours.">
    <meta property="og:image" content="https://www.example.com/images/apple-banner.jpg">
    <meta property="og:url" content="https://www.example.com/organic-apples">

title: Chapter 11: Embedded Content, SVGs, Canvas, and Scripts
summary: Learn how to embed complex content into HTML. We cover adding JavaScript using the <script> tag (and async/defer attributes), drawing graphics with <canvas> and <svg>, and handling users with JS disabled.
content: ## Adding JavaScript: The `<script>` Tag

To make HTML interactive, you must attach JavaScript. The `<script>` tag is used either to write JS directly inside the HTML or to link to an external `.js` file.

**Where to put the `<script>` tag?**
Historically, scripts were placed at the very bottom of the `<body>` so they wouldn't block the HTML from rendering. Today, it is best practice to place them in the `<head>` and use the `defer` or `async` attributes.
## `defer` vs `async`

- `defer`: The script is downloaded in the background while the HTML parses. It is guaranteed to execute *only after* the HTML is fully parsed, and in the order the scripts appear. **(Recommended for most scripts)**.
- `async`: The script is downloaded in the background and executes *the exact millisecond* it finishes downloading, pausing HTML parsing to do so. Use this only for independent scripts like Google Analytics.
## The `<noscript>` Tag
What if a user has JavaScript disabled in their browser? The `<noscript>` tag displays alternative content (usually a warning) only when JS is turned off.
## Scalable Vector Graphics: `<svg>`

SVGs are images defined in XML format. Unlike JPEGs or PNGs, SVGs are infinitely scalable without losing quality and have very small file sizes. You can embed the `<svg>` code directly into your HTML, allowing you to style the image using CSS (e.g., changing its color on hover).
## The `<canvas>` Element
The `<canvas>` element provides an empty space on the page where you can draw graphics, animations, or even 3D games "on the fly" using JavaScript.
## The `<template>` and `<slot>` Tags (Web Components)

The `<template>` tag holds HTML content that is *not* rendered immediately when the page loads. It is stored invisibly, waiting for JavaScript to clone it and insert it into the DOM. This is the foundation of Web Components.

title: Chapter 12: HTML Attributes Masterclass — Global Attributes & Data Attributes
summary: Discover the hidden power of HTML attributes. Learn about global attributes that can be applied to any element, custom data-* attributes for JavaScript data storage, and accessibility-focused aria-* attributes.
content: ## What are Global Attributes?
While some attributes are specific to certain tags (like `src` on an ``), **Global Attributes** can be applied to *any* HTML element.
## Core Global Attributes

- `id`: Specifies a unique identifier for an element. Cannot be repeated on the page.
- `class`: Specifies one or more class names for an element (used by CSS and JS). Can be used on multiple elements.
- `style`: Applies inline CSS styling directly to the element. (Best practice is to use external CSS instead).
- `title`: Provides extra information about an element, typically displayed as a tooltip when the mouse hovers over it.
## Interactive and State Attributes

- `hidden`: A boolean attribute. When present, the browser will not display the element. It is functionally equivalent to CSS `display: none`.
- `tabindex`: Specifies the tabbing order of an element. `tabindex="0"` makes a non-focusable element (like a `<div>`) focusable via the keyboard. `tabindex="-1"` removes an element from the keyboard navigation flow.
- `contenteditable`: Set to `true` to allow the user to edit the text directly inside the browser! (This is how rich text editors are built).
- `draggable`: Set to `true` to specify whether an element is draggable (using the HTML5 Drag and Drop API).
- `spellcheck`: Set to `true` or `false` to specify whether the element should have its spelling and grammar checked by the browser.
## Custom Data Attributes (`data-*`)

Sometimes you need to attach custom data to an HTML element so your JavaScript can read it later. You cannot just invent attributes (like `my-custom-id="123"`) because it makes the HTML invalid.

Instead, use the `data-*` prefix. Anything starting with `data-` is completely valid HTML5.
## ARIA Attributes (`aria-*`)

WAI-ARIA (Web Accessibility Initiative - Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attributes provide extra context to screen readers for complex widgets that don't have native HTML equivalents (like custom dropdowns or modal dialogs).
